b: Home
o: An iPhone and iPad app that follows your breathing rhythm through the microphone and scores your session. A relaxation and focus exercise.
g: FOR IPHONE AND IPAD An app that hears your breath. Most apps run a timer. Soluklan listens to your exhale and your inhale through the microphone, and shows you cycle by cycle how closely you kept to the rhythm. Download on the App Store Browse the guide A relaxation and focus exercise. It does not offer medical diagnosis, treatment or advice. 5.5 seconds in · 5.5 seconds out WHAT IS MEASURED An app that can't hear your breath is only a timer. In every cycle Soluklan measures when your exhale began, how long it lasted and how steady its sound was. When the session ends you are left with a measurement, not an impression. threshold noise floor exhale The app keeps no audio file. All it has is this line: the sound level, measured every twenty milliseconds. The threshold is set from how quiet the room is. HOW IT WORKS It listens, measures and tells you. You follow the circle Breathe in as it grows, out as it shrinks. The circle does whatever the technique says: it waits if there is a hold, and shrinks slowly if the exhale is long. The microphone hears your breath Only the instant sound level is worked out from the audio. Which cycle you were late on, how long your exhale lasted, how steady its sound was, whether air escaped during a hold — all of it is measured. A report arrives at the end A score out of a hundred, a short headline, what you did well and a few concrete suggestions. If you want, you can open every measurement and read them one by one. 84 The score isn't a single measurement: rhythm match, exhales heard, exhale length, inhale, breath volume, how smooth the exhale was and completion are worked out together. TECHNIQUES Sixteen techniques, all well-known methods. Coherent, Box, Triangle, Deep and Slow, Extended Exhale, Physiological Sigh, 4-7-8, Pursed Lip, Energizing, Humming Bee, Ocean, Alternate Nostril, Left Nostril, Right Nostril, Cooling and Kapalabhati. Each one comes with what it is good for, how to do it, the mistakes people make and a single guided round to try. Where the evidence is thin, we say so plainly. The circle works like it does in the app: breathe in as it grows, out as it shrinks. No sound, no measuring, nothing recorded. Set up a program and you do the same technique for the same length every day. The app keeps track of which day you are on and warns you if you start missing. When it ends it lays out day by day what happened: which days slipped, how your scores moved, which suggestions kept coming back. Twenty-eight days, five minutes a day. Filled days are the ones you did, the empty one slipped. Today is day seventeen. KEEPING IT UP It makes the habit easier. Streak and milestones How many days in a row you practised is marked on the calendar. There are stops along the way — three days, a week, two weeks, a month — and the app celebrates each one you reach. Next to these ready-made stops you can set your own: say “forty days” and that gets marked on the calendar too. Suggestions made for you The suggested length isn't a single number but a range that moves with your experience and your recent sessions. The order of the techniques changes with what you have already done today. Reminders are yours to set Which day at which time, how many a day at most, quiet hours, holiday mode and reminder texts you write yourself. More detail → THE LOOK The app changes as the day goes by. The background is light and open from sunrise to sunset, warm orange in the evening, dark and starry at night. Sunrise and sunset are worked out on your device — no location permission is asked for. Day Evening Night Winter Spring Autumn Summer has a background of its own, and special days like New Year get their own looks. The season comes from the calendar; nothing is fetched from the internet. PLATFORM SUPPORT Full size on the phone and on the tablet. If you like a big screen, there is a tablet version too. FREQUENTLY ASKED Short answers Under every answer there is a link to the article that covers it in full. Do I need the microphone, can I turn it off? You don't need it. With the microphone on, the app hears your breath, measures how closely you follow the rhythm and gives you a score. With it off, the circle, the rhythm, the haptics, your streak, milestones and programs all work exactly the same — only the score isn't worked out. You can tap "Continue without the microphone" when a session starts, or turn it off completely in Settings. More: If your breath isn't being heard → Is audio recorded? No. The microphone runs only during a session and only the instant sound level is worked out from it — no audio file is written to disk. The one exception is the audio sample sharing you give separate permission for. If you haven't turned that on, audio is never recorded in any session. More: Managing your data → My breath isn't being heard, what should I do? In order: hold the device 20-30 cm from your mouth, don't cover the microphone, pick a quiet place, and don't move while it says "Measuring the room" at the start of a session. Don't force your breath to make it louder — that doesn't fix the measurement, it spoils it. More: If your breath isn't being heard → How is the score worked out? Several separate measurements are combined: rhythm match, exhales heard, exhale length, inhale, breath volume, how smooth the exhale was, and whether you completed the session. They don't all carry the same weight; the largest share goes to rhythm match. More: How a session is scored → What are the short lines that appear during a session? Notes that show up under the circle and fade after a few seconds: "A little late", "Your breath is hard to hear", "Air escaped during the hold" and so on. They point at things you can still fix before the session ends, and well-timed cycles get praise too. They don't come often: never during the first cycle or in the last seconds, at least ten seconds between two of them, and the same sentence twice at most. They look at the same threshold as the measurement behind the report, so they never contradict it. More: What's on the session screen → I got a low score, am I doing it wrong? A low score doesn't mean you are breathing wrong. The score only measures how closely you followed the pace on screen — not whether the breathing did you good. And the measurement relies on the microphone: sitting far from the device, or a noisy room, can make a perfectly good session look low. Tap "Detailed report" and you'll see which measurement dropped and what to fix. More: Reading your session report → See all How many minutes should a session be? Even two minutes helps. The lit band on the length slider is the range suggested for you: it shifts with your experience, your recent sessions, the time of day and your streak. A short session you finish beats a long one you abandon, by every measure. More: Choosing a technique and a length → Why are techniques locked, and how do they open? The path runs from easy to hard: you start with techniques that have no hold, move on to holds, then to the advanced ones. Tap a locked card and it tells you what is needed and the shortest way there. If you marked your experience level high in the intake, most locks are open from the start. More: Unlocking techniques → Which technique should I do when? 4-7-8 or Extended Exhale before sleep, Box or Triangle during a work break, Physiological Sigh for sudden tension, Energizing Breath or Right Nostril when you feel dull. If you can't decide, take the suggestion at the top of the list: it is chosen from your goal, the time of day and your recent sessions. More: Which technique, and when → How does the streak work, and what if I miss a day? The streak counts how many days in a row you did a session. Missing a day resets it, but your longest streak stays on record and a new streak starts the next day. Doing several sessions in one day doesn't speed the streak up: it counts days, not sessions. More: Streak, milestones and the calendar → I'm taking a break for a while — is my streak safe? Yes. Turn on Settings → Notification options → Holiday mode: notifications go quiet until the date you set and your streak is preserved. One warning: holiday mode ends an active program , because a program keeps counting days. The app asks you about this before switching to holiday mode. More: Streak, milestones and the calendar → What is a program, and how is it different from a streak? A streak asks "did you do something today"; a program asks "how many days have you done the same technique for the same length". The measured effects come from the second one. The first program is twenty-eight days, five minutes a day — that is the length used in the study the program is based on. b: Privacy
o: Soluklan privacy policy: audio is never recorded, session data stays on your device, no ads and no tracking.
g: Privacy Policy Last updated: 24 August 2026 In short Your session records are kept on your device and backed up in your own iCloud account . We cannot reach that data. Your audio is never written to disk . The microphone runs only during a session, and only the instant sound level is worked out from it — how that works . No ads, no tracking, no third-party analytics. We have written separately on why there is no third-party code inside the app. You can optionally share an anonymous session summary and, now and then , an audio sample. You are asked about each separately and can turn either off whenever you like. Everything about what is kept where is in Managing your data . Data that stays on your device Session summaries (date, technique, length, score, report), your intake answers (goal, experience, preferred time of day, health notes), your settings and your notification preferences are stored on your device. If iCloud is on, this data syncs in your own account on Apple's iCloud infrastructure; as the developer we have no access to that area. If you delete the app, the data on the device is deleted; for the iCloud copy you can use Apple's iCloud settings. Optional sharing Anonymous session summary. If you turn it on, the following is sent: a randomly generated anonymous identifier, the date and time zone (not the minute or second), the technique, the length, the score, whether the session was completed, whether the microphone was used, the app version and the technical values from the session report. Your name, email address, phone number, location, device identifier and health answers are never sent. The anonymous identifier is generated inside the app only and cannot be matched to a person or to an iCloud account. Feedback. With anonymous sharing on, a short question appears at the end of a session now and then: a score out of ten, followed by one more question. Both the score and the text can be skipped. What is sent: the score you gave, the text you wrote , the technique, the length, the session score, whether the session was completed, whether the microphone was used, the app version, the date and the anonymous identifier above. The text you write is free text and is read by us ; don't write anything in the box that gives away who you are. Name, email address, location and health answers are not sent here either. With anonymous sharing off, this question is never asked. Audio sample. If you give separate permission, the audio of a few sessions (at most five a day) is sent in compressed form. This option is never shown to anyone who says they are under 13: in many countries a file containing a child's voice counts as personal data. If you did not give your age in the intake, a warning appears under the option. Its only purpose is to measure and improve the accuracy of breath detection; we have described how the thresholds are measured against real recordings in a separate article. The file that is sent is deleted from your device. If you turn this permission off, any pending audio files are deleted too. Shared data is stored on Apple CloudKit and used only to develop the app. It is not sold or transferred to third parties. What we do with each record that arrives is in What we do with the data you share . Permissions Microphone: to detect your breath. Audio is not recorded (only if you turn on the audio sample permission above is it recorded, and only in those sessions). Notifications: only for the reminders you set up yourself. Notifications are scheduled on your device, not sent from a server — which notification arrives when . Children The app is not directed at children and does not knowingly collect data from children. Your rights You can turn sharing off at any time in Settings → Privacy; deleting your data is in the same place. If you want records already sent to be deleted, writing to the address below is enough; if you pass on your anonymous identifier from the app, the matching records will be deleted. Contact Email: info@soluklan.app

b: Alternate Nostril Breathing
o: In left, out right, in right, out left. The technique in the app that demands the most coordination, and how the finger position settles.
g: You close the nostrils in turn with your right hand: in through the left, out through the right, in through the right, out through the left. Each step is four seconds. Four steps make one cycle. Its Sanskrit name is Nadi Shodhana. It is the technique in the app that asks for the most attention. What it is good for Breathing through one nostril slows the airflow — you get a long breath without forcing it. Second, and more noticeable in practice: following the finger, the nostril and the rhythm at the same time leaves the mind no room for anything else. That is why it is one of the best techniques to do with a scattered mind. Studies have reported that it increases heart rate variability and lowers blood pressure slightly. These findings are consistent with the general effects of slow breathing. The finger position Use your right hand. Your thumb closes the right nostril and your ring finger the left . The index and middle fingers curl towards the palm or rest on your forehead. The order goes like this: 1. Close the right with the thumb, breathe in through the left for four seconds . 2. Close the left with the ring finger, lift the thumb, breathe out through the right for four seconds . 3. With the same hand, breathe in through the right for four seconds . 4. Close the right with the thumb, breathe out through the left for four seconds . Cycle complete. In the app the label under the circle tells you which nostril to use at every step — you don't have to memorise it. Common mistakes Not closing the nostril fully. The finger should press lightly but completely. Air seeps through a half-closed nostril and the technique loses its point. Rushing. Keep each step going until the circle finishes. Don't cut the breath to move your finger. Forcing the breath. Air enters more slowly through one nostril. What you take in over four seconds will be less than through two nostrils, and that is normal. Why it is one of the last to unlock In the app this technique is at an advanced level. You are asked to do Left or Right Nostril Breathing first. The reason: getting used to breathing through a single nostril is far easier than learning the finger position and the four-step order at the same time. Once single-nostril settles, the alternating form comes by itself. How the app measures it Breathing through one nostril is very quiet. The app uses one of its most sensitive thresholds for this technique and can still find it hard to hear. The first step of the tutorial says so directly: move somewhere quiet, because background sound spoils the measurement in this technique. Hold the device near your nose. The microphone hearing little is normal here. Who should take care If your nose is blocked, don't force it. No other known risk — there is no hold and no fast breathing.

b: Backgrounds, seasons and the time of day
o: The background changing through the day isn't decoration. How it is worked out, why it asks for no location data, and what appears when.
g: Open the app in the morning and the background is light and open; in the late afternoon it is warm orange; at night it is dark and starry. Snow falls in winter and leaves drift down in spring. Here is what sits behind that. Why it exists Two reasons. The first is that it tells you what time of day it is the moment you open the app — breathing practice is tied to the time of day, and the app already changes its suggestions with the hour. The background is the visible side of that. The second is simpler: an app you open every day doesn't have to look the same every day. The sun's hours are worked out on the device Sunrise and sunset aren't fixed hours; they shift with the season. The app works them out. It asks for no location permission. The calculation is made from the device's time zone; GPS and location services are never touched. That means giving up a little accuracy — a few minutes of drift is possible — but there is no good reason for a breathing app to ask for your location. The times of day Day. From sunrise to sunset, light and open. Evening. Around sunset, warm orange tones. Night. A dark background and stars. Some of the stars fade and brighten faster than others, and a few are faintly coloured. The seasons Winter. Snowflakes. A background in cold blue tones. Spring. Falling blossom petals. Summer. A calm background leaning towards green. Autumn. Yellow and red leaves. The season comes from the calendar date, not from the weather — the app doesn't look at the internet. Special days A few special days like New Year get their own backgrounds. These come and go by date, by themselves. Light and dark themes On top of all this there is a theme choice: Settings → Appearance. It shouldn't be confused with the interface level . You can follow the system setting, or always use the light or dark theme. In the dark theme the night background stays close to its default; in the light theme the day background stays light even at night. Reduce motion If iOS's reduce motion setting is on, the snow, leaves and star movements stop. The background colours stay; the motion goes. The same setting also affects the animations in the session circle and on this site. Does it drain the battery The background animations are drawn only while the app is in the foreground, at a low frame rate, and never in the background. During a session, when the circle is on screen, priority goes to that anyway.

b: Box Breathing
o: Four equal steps: in, hold, out, hold. Four breaths a minute. The technique most widely taught in military and emergency service training.
g: Four seconds in, four held, four out, four waiting. Then from the top. Four equal sides. The name comes from the shape: draw it on paper and you get a square. What it is good for The two holds bring the breath down to four a minute. That is less than half the resting rate of a calm person. Slowness itself is a signal in the body: someone breathing at this rate isn't running and isn't being chased. Its second job, and perhaps the more important one, is about attention. You have to count all four steps and can't let any of them slide. There is no gap left for the mind to wander into. This technique is widely taught in military and emergency service training. The reason isn't complicated physiology but its simplicity: easy to count, doable standing up, no equipment needed. Where the evidence stands There are few controlled studies done directly on box breathing. The best comparison we have is the 2023 study described in the article on the physiological sigh : box breathing was there as a one-month practice arm and showed improvement in mood measures — behind the sigh, but ahead of where it started. The general effects of slow breathing apply to this technique too. Claims beyond that — "resets your stress", "doubles your focus" — don't come from the studies. How to do it Sit upright, feet on the floor. Breathe in through the nose for four seconds, letting the belly rise. Hold for four seconds. Don't lock your throat, just stop. Breathe out through the nose for four seconds — not by blowing, but quietly and evenly. Wait four seconds with empty lungs. This is the hardest step. If waiting is uncomfortable, shorten the length. Common mistakes Lifting the shoulders on the inhale. The breath should go to the belly, not the chest. Put a hand on your belly: let that be what rises. Locking the throat during the hold. Closing the airway creates pressure and makes the hold harder. Just stop. Struggling with the second hold. Waiting with empty lungs feels hard to most people. If you struggle, work on Triangle Breathing first — that second hold isn't there. How the app measures it There are two separate hold windows and both are measured separately. It shows in the report as hold cleanliness: in how many cycles no air escaped. The most common leak is in the empty hold — a small amount of air seeping out when the breath isn't finished. This usually comes from ending the exhale early instead of spreading it across the four seconds. Who should take care If you get dizzy during a hold, skip it. Long holds can be uncomfortable for people with blood pressure problems; shortening the length or choosing a technique without holds is better. Source Balban et al. (2023), Cell Reports Medicine — the comparative study in which box breathing was one of the arms. Full text

b: If your breath isn't being heard
o: What to try, in order, when you see "No exhale was heard". Distance, the room, the difference between devices, and carrying on without the microphone.
g: If the app can't hear your breath, the session doesn't become useless — but the score becomes meaningless. The cause is usually one of a few things. Let's go through them in order. 1. Distance This is the most common cause. Hold the device 20-30 cm from your mouth and nose. If you laid it flat on a table, the microphone is most likely facing sideways rather than up. Propping the phone against a book, or holding it, makes a clear difference. Know where the microphone is: on an iPhone it is on the bottom edge, next to the charging port. If your hand covers it, nothing is heard. 2. The room There is a three-second measurement at the start of a session — while the screen says "Measuring the room…", don't talk and don't move . A sound in that moment is taken for room noise, and the threshold stays wrong for the whole session. A television, air conditioning, a fan, an open window: all of them raise the threshold. A quiet room is best. 3. Your exhale really being very quiet Some techniques are quiet by nature. A breath out through a single nostril is the quietest of all; Coherent and Deep and Slow are low too. The app knows this and uses a different threshold for each technique. But it varies from person to person as well: some people's nasal exhale really is very quiet. The fix is not to force the breath. Pushing to make the exhale stronger both spoils the technique and lowers the "breath volume" measurement. Bring the device closer instead. 4. If you are using a tablet On a tablet the microphone array is wide and the input level comes out noticeably lower than on a phone. In one tablet recording, the highest point of the exhale was far below even the quietest of the phone recordings. On a tablet the app picks the microphone source nearest your mouth, but the gap doesn't close completely. On a tablet you need to hold it closer. 5. Look at what the report says Under Detailed report there is an "Exhale peak level" line: something like "20 dB above the floor". If that difference is under 10 dB , the sound really is too weak — work on distance and the room. If it is 20 dB or more , the sound is enough and the problem may be elsewhere (timing, for instance). If the line isn't there at all, no measurable exhale was found in that session. 6. Microphone permission If Breath detection (microphone) is off in Settings, nothing is measured. If you denied the permission in iOS's Settings app, the app says so and shows a button that takes you straight there. You can do a session without the microphone If none of this helps, or you simply don't feel like it, carry on without the microphone: Continue without the microphone when the session starts, or turn the microphone off entirely in Settings. In a session without the microphone no score is worked out, but the circle, the rhythm, the haptics, your streak, milestones and programs all work exactly the same. The report says it was a "session without the microphone", and the session still counts towards your streak. One more thing If the app doesn't hear your exhale for a while during a session, it shows a short warning. That warning uses the same threshold as the measurement: it won't say "not being heard" on screen and "heard" in the report. If you are seeing the warning, it really can't measure it.

b: Building the habit: the first thirty days
o: Where the difference is made between using the app for a week and keeping it up for thirty days. A plan broken into weeks.
g: The hard part of a breathing practice isn't learning the technique, it is keeping it up. Tools like the streak, milestones , programs and reminders exist for exactly that. Here is how to use them, week by week. Week one: get to know one technique This week the aim is learning , not scoring well. Take the technique suggested in the intake and do it for a week. Read its tutorial from start to finish, and don't skip the hands-on round. Keep the length short: two minutes. Two minutes finished every day is worth far more than ten minutes done once. Set the reminder today. If you put it off, it doesn't get set. This week's measure: a session on at least five of the seven days. Week two: start making sense of the measurements Once the technique settles, start looking at the report. Open Detailed report and see which component is low. For most people the first thing to improve is rhythm match : learning to wait for the moment the circle starts shrinking takes a few sessions. Stretch the length a little. The lit band on the slider will already have shifted to suit you. This week's measure: your average score in the same technique rising against last week. The weekly summary shows this directly. Week three: add a second technique You now know one technique. A second should have unlocked — tap one of the locked cards and look at the shortest way. Split the two: use one for the morning and the other for the evening . The app already suggests by time of day. This week's measure: at least three sessions in each of two different techniques. Week four: set up a program This week is the real step. Profile → Programs , and start the twenty-eight day program. Here is what makes a program different: a streak asks "did you do something today", while a program asks "how many days have you done the same thing for the same length". The measured effects come from the second one. While a program runs, your reminder tells you the program's day and that technique moves to the top of the technique list. This week's measure: completing the program's first seven days without a miss. The days you miss You will miss days. The problem isn't missing one, it is quitting after you do. If you missed one day , come back the next with a short session. Your streak may have reset, but your longest streak stays on record. If you missed several days in a row and you have a program, the program may have ended. An ended program goes to your history and how far you got stays there — it isn't wiped. If you know you'll be away for a week , turn on holiday mode : your streak is preserved. But an active program ends, so do it knowing that. At the end of thirty days The program's finishing screen tells you how many days, how many sessions and how many minutes you did. The program breakdown shows which days you missed, which day of the week is hard for you, and how your scores changed from the first half to the second. That breakdown is the best guide for your next program: knowing that "Tuesdays always slip" means putting a separate reminder on Tuesday. The real trick to keeping it up On hard days, shorten the length, don't skip the day . A two-minute session completes the day, keeps the streak and completes the program's day. What breaks a habit isn't a bad session, it is a day with none at all.

b: Coherent Breathing
o: Five and a half breaths a minute. The most studied, the easiest to learn, and open from the start in the app. Why this speed, and what the evidence actually shows.
g: Five and a half seconds in, five and a half seconds out. No hold, no mouth, no effort. That comes to about five and a half breaths a minute. That is the whole thing. The technique has no trick to teach — the difficulty is keeping it up without getting bored. Why this speed There is a relationship between breathing speed and the heartbeat: the heart speeds up as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out. Everyone has this rise and fall, and it is taken as a sign of health. When you breathe at close to six breaths a minute, that rise and fall lines up with the circulatory system's own rhythm and heart rate variability increases markedly. It is a measurable, repeatable effect. The best speed shifts a little from person to person — five breaths a minute for some, six and a half for others. The " your own pace " part of the app exists precisely to find it. Five and a half is a reasonable starting point for the average. Once you move to your own pace, the app pulls it to the value you measured. What you can expect The increase in heart rate variability is well demonstrated. Claims beyond that — reducing anxiety, lowering blood pressure, improving sleep — sit on a messier picture: some studies find an effect, others don't, participant numbers are mostly small and the comparison groups are weak. So "your heart rate variability goes up" and "your anxiety goes away" are not sentences of equal reliability. The app keeps the two apart. In practice what most people report is more modest: after a few minutes the shoulders drop and the mind slows a little. That is not nothing. How to do it Sit upright or lie on your back. Keep your mouth closed, breathe in through the nose and out through the nose. Breathe in as the circle grows: let the belly widen first, the chest after. Breathe out as it shrinks: don't push the breath, let it go. The exhale should be free , not muscular. There is no hold. There is no pause between breaths either — as the exhale ends, the inhale begins. The flow should be unbroken. Common mistakes Taking it for deep breathing. Coherent breathing isn't deep breathing, it is slow breathing. If you try to fill your lungs completely, five and a half seconds will feel long and you will struggle. Normal volume, just slow. Forcing the exhale. Pushing the exhale out with muscle is the most common mistake. The app hears it: the sound comes out louder than it should and the report says "let the breath go, don't push". Breathing from the shoulders. If your shoulders rise, you are breathing from the chest. Put a hand on your belly; the movement should come from there. How the app measures it Coherent is a calm technique breathed out through the nose, so the sound is low. The thresholds are set accordingly — listened to with the threshold of a mouth-exhale technique, nothing would be heard at all. What gets measured: whether the exhale starts at the same moment as the circle, how long it lasts, how steady the sound level stays through the exhale, and whether the inhale was heard. There is no hold phase, so there is no hold measurement. Not hearing the inhale at all is normal: a nasal inhale really can be silent. It has a small share of the score, so on its own it doesn't sink a session. Who should take care This technique has no known risk; it is one of the gentlest in the app, which is why it is open from the start. Even so, the rule that applies to every breathing exercise applies here: if you feel dizzy, stop and go back to your normal breathing. If slow breathing is new to you, there can be a mild feeling of air hunger in the first minutes, and that usually passes within a few sessions. Sources Lehrer et al. (2020), Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback — a review and meta-analysis of heart rate variability biofeedback. PubMed Zaccaro et al. (2018), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience — a wide-ranging review of the effects of slow breathing. Full text

b: Cooling Breath
o: Air drawn between the teeth leaves a coolness in the mouth. Tradition calls it "cooling", but measurement doesn't bear that out — we write both.
g: Close your teeth lightly together and part your lips. Draw air slowly through that narrow gap for four seconds. Then close your mouth and breathe out through the nose over six seconds. The sound happens only on the inhale: a soft hiss. The exhale is silent. What happens When air passes through a narrow gap, the inhale slows by itself — you get a long inhale without having to force it. Second, as the air passes through your wet mouth there is evaporation, and that leaves a clear coolness. You feel it on your teeth and on your tongue. The "cooling" question The classical texts describe this technique as cooling. In a study of seventeen people, body temperature was measured and it did not drop ; it rose slightly. So the coolness you feel in your mouth is a real sensation, but it isn't cooling your body. We write it that way both in the app and on the site: the sentence "it cools the body" appears nowhere. That it feels good on a hot day or when you are angry may come from that sensation and from the slowed breathing. We have no more than a single study with a small number of participants. How to do it Close your teeth lightly — don't clench , just let them touch. Part your lips as if smiling, leaving a thin gap between the teeth. Draw air slowly through that gap for four seconds. You'll hear a hiss. Close your mouth and breathe out through the nose for six seconds. The version with the tongue If you can curl your tongue into a tube and put its tip out between your lips, you can do the same thing with the tongue. Because the gap is narrower, the coolness feels a little stronger — classically called Sitali. Not everyone's tongue curls; that is inherited. If yours doesn't, don't worry about it: the version with the teeth is the same technique, and it is the one the app is built around. Common mistakes Drawing the air in fast. Drawing fast dries the throat and brings on a cough. Draw slowly. Clenching the teeth. Touching is enough; keep your jaw loose. Breathing out through the mouth. The exhale is always through the nose, mouth closed. Doing it in very cold air. Don't do it outdoors in winter or in front of an air conditioner. How the app measures it This technique reverses the usual arrangement in the app: the noise is on the inhale and the exhale is silent. In the other techniques the exhale is strong and the inhale is low. Here it is exactly the other way round, so the app is lenient on the exhale and takes its real measurement from the hiss of the inhale. This technique's thresholds haven't yet been measured against real recordings — it is running on initial values. If you turned audio sample sharing on, the sessions you do help this setting settle directly. Who should take care If you have asthma or are sensitive to cold, be careful: cold, dry air can irritate the airways. The app shows this warning before the session. When your throat dries out, take a break and drink some water. Sources Hatha Yoga Pradipika (15th century, chapter 2) — verse 54 describes the version with the teeth, verses 57-58 the one with the tongue. Telles et al. (2020), Medical Science Monitor Basic Research — body temperature, oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide output measured in seventeen people; temperature did not drop. PubMed

b: Deep and Slow
o: Six seconds in, six seconds out. No hold, no ornament. The best technique for learning to use the diaphragm.
g: Six seconds in through the nose, six seconds out through the nose. Five breaths a minute. It looks a lot like Coherent Breathing . The difference is that the pace is a little slower and the emphasis is on depth . What it is good for This technique teaches diaphragmatic breathing. Most people breathe through the upper chest all day: the shoulders lift slightly and the belly doesn't move. That is a fast, shallow pattern. The diaphragm — the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs — pulls the lower part of the lung open when it contracts. Because blood flow is denser in the lower part, taking oxygen from the air is more efficient there too. Five breaths a minute is in the range where the measured effects of slow breathing appear: heart rate variability increases and the breathing rate drops. How to do it Put a hand on your belly. In this technique your hand is the best teacher. Breathe in through the nose for six seconds. Let your belly be what rises , not your shoulders. It can feel strange in the first sessions — it is the opposite of the habit. Breathe out through the nose for six seconds. Don't push; let it go — the belly draws in by itself. No hold, no waiting. Common mistakes Breathing with the chest. The most widespread mistake. If the hand on your belly doesn't rise, you are breathing from the chest. Forcing the exhale out. Pushing the air out with the abdominal muscles is unnecessary. When the diaphragm relaxes, the air leaves by itself. Taking in too much. The word "deep" misleads: it doesn't mean filling until you burst, it means reaching down to the lower part. Six seconds should pass comfortably. How it differs from Coherent In practice the two are very close. Coherent focuses more on rhythm (five and a half a minute, breath matched with heartbeat); Deep and Slow on depth (the diaphragm working). Both are open from the start in the app. If you want to settle belly breathing, Deep and Slow suits better; if you want to settle the rhythm, Coherent. How the app measures it A calm technique breathed out through the nose, so the sound is low. With no hold, the measurement is simple: the timing, the length and the smoothness of the exhale, and whether the inhale was heard. In this technique the sound of the exhale comes out very low for most people. If it isn't heard, bringing the device a little closer is enough. Forcing the breath to make it audible is not the right fix: the measurement gets spoiled and the technique loses its point. Who should take care No known risk. If six seconds feels long, drop to five — what matters is that the rhythm is even and unbroken.

b: The Energizing Breath
o: Two seconds in, two seconds out. The only technique in the app with a locked length — it can't go past one minute, and there is a good reason for that.
g: Take a lively two-second breath in through the nose, then two seconds out. Fifteen breaths a minute — above the normal resting rate. Every other technique in the app slows the breath down. This one speeds it up. What it is good for Fast, even breathing lowers the carbon dioxide in the blood for a short time. That produces a feeling of alertness and liveliness — in some people it is also felt as a mild tingling or lightness in the head. The effect is brief. Don't think of it as coffee: it is closer to splashing cold water on your face. Why the length is locked In the app this technique is capped at one minute and the slider doesn't go past it. No other technique has a lock like this. The reason: when fast breathing goes on for longer, the drop in carbon dioxide becomes pronounced and can cause dizziness, tingling, numbness in the hands and around the mouth, and in some people a dimming of vision. One minute is enough for the alerting effect and short of those symptoms. We lock the length because the reflex "that felt good, let me do a bit more" is exactly what's dangerous here. How to do it Sit upright. Take a lively two-second breath in through the nose — lively, not deep . Breathe out through the nose for two seconds. Keep the rhythm lively but unforced. When the time is up, return to normal breathing and wait a few breaths. Common mistakes Breathing too deeply as well as fast. Breathing both fast and deep speeds up the drop in carbon dioxide. Keep the breaths small. Standing up straight afterwards. When you finish, take a few normal breaths before you move. Who shouldn't do it The app steers away from this technique in these situations: asthma or a respiratory condition, a heart condition, pregnancy, a tendency to dizziness. The card drops to the bottom and a warning appears. It is also suggested for the morning, and it drops out of the suggestions at night with the note "not suitable for the night; it may keep you awake". For users over sixty-five and under thirteen it also moves down the order, with a separate note. How the app measures it The windows are narrow: a two-second inhale, a two-second exhale. That is a demanding case for the detector — telling that an exhale has ended needs a short silence afterwards, and here that silence is very short. So this technique has one of the lowest thresholds in the app, and the end of an exhale is decided by a silence condition together with a "fall from the peak" condition. These were measured and tuned against real recordings.

b: Extended Exhale
o: Four in, four held, eight out. Stretching the exhale to twice the inhale rests on one of the most consistently measured effects among breathing techniques.
g: Four seconds in through the nose. Hold for four. Breathe out slowly through the mouth over eight seconds. The exhale being longer than the inhale is the whole logic of this technique. Why a long exhale Heart rate swings with the breath: it speeds up as you breathe in and slows as you breathe out. In a healthy heart this is expected. Lengthening the exhale means lengthening the part where the heart slows. In measurements this shows as the average heart rate falling and heart rate variability rising. It is one of the most consistently demonstrated effects among breathing techniques. The sentence "a long exhale slows the heart" stands on far firmer ground than "a long exhale takes anxiety away". How to do it Sit upright. Breathe in through the nose for four seconds — not enough to burst your lungs, just enough to last eight seconds. Hold for four seconds. Breathe out through the mouth for eight seconds. As if blowing out a candle, but without blowing: lips slightly parted, the air leaving thin and quiet. Common mistakes Finishing the exhale at the fifth second. The most common problem. The cause is usually not taking in too little on the inhale but emptying too fast at the start. Give less in the first second and spread the rest to the end. Blowing. Forcing the air out speeds the exhale up and takes the effect away. Let the air leave by itself. Getting stuck on eight seconds. If eight feels long, drop to six. What matters isn't the number but the exhale being clearly longer than the inhale. How the app measures it The exhale is through the mouth, so the sound is strong — this is one of the techniques the app measures most comfortably. What gets measured: how long the exhale lasts, how steady the sound level stays through it, and whether air escaped during the hold. Exhale length is the component that drops most often in this technique. If that line comes out low in the report, the first place to look is whether the exhale is emptying too fast at the start. Who should take care If you feel dizzy during a long exhale, shorten the length. For people who mark a tendency to dizziness, the app steers away from this technique and shows a warning — the technique isn't hidden, but it moves down the order.

b: Finding your own pace
o: The five and a half seconds of Coherent Breathing is an average. You can measure the breathing speed that suits you best and have the app run at it.
g: By default Coherent Breathing runs at five and a half seconds in, five and a half seconds out. That is an average. The match between breathing speed and the heart's rhythm doesn't peak at the same speed for everyone: for some it is five breaths a minute, for others six and a half. The app can measure this for you. The measurement settings When you pick Coherent Breathing in the technique list , a line appears underneath: find your own pace. Before it starts, two things are asked. Length of the measurement. Full measurement tries five paces for two minutes each — the route the scientific method takes, and the most reliable result. Quick try tries three paces for a minute and a half each; it is over faster, and the result is a little rougher. How to measure. With mic works the result out from how evenly your breath follows the rhythm. No mic doesn't measure at all: you try the paces in turn and decide yourself which one feels comfortable. How the measurement works The measurement tries several different speeds in turn. At each speed you breathe for a short while, and the app measures how evenly your breath holds that speed. While it runs, the screen tells you which speed you are on. Tap End the measurement and the result up to that point is used; tap Restart the measurement and it starts over. The result When the measurement finishes, the value it found is saved and Coherent Breathing runs at that speed from then on. It appears in Settings on the Coherent Breathing pace row, with a note saying where it came from: Found by measurement or Set manually . If you don't like it you can change it by hand. When you try to, the app asks once — because you are writing over a value that was measured. When to measure again Your resonance pace isn't something that changes quickly. Measuring again after a few months, or after a stretch of regular practice, can make sense. Don't measure on a day when you are ill, very tired, or have just exercised — the result will reflect that day's state. It isn't required Coherent Breathing works without the measurement. Five and a half seconds is a reasonable value for most people. This measurement is for anyone who wants a little more from their breathing. While measuring Do it somewhere quiet with the microphone on. The measurement relies on hearing your breath; if it can't be heard, the result won't be reliable. The measurement takes a few minutes. If you cut it short, a result is worked out from the data so far, but it isn't as reliable as a full measurement.

b: 4-7-8 Breathing
o: Four in, seven held, eight out. The longest hold in the app is here. A technique whose popularity outruns its evidence — and we say so plainly.
g: Breathe in through the nose for four seconds. Hold for seven. Breathe out through the mouth for eight seconds with pursed lips, making an "ffff" sound. One cycle takes nineteen seconds. The longest hold in the app is in this technique. What it is good for Two things work at once. The exhale is twice the inhale — so the logic of Extended Exhale is here too: the heart slows on the exhale, and lengthening the exhale enlarges that slowing. The long hold raises the carbon dioxide in the blood a little. Because that increases the urge to breathe, it can feel uncomfortable in the first sessions, but with practice a tolerance for slow breathing develops. Where the evidence stands — let's be honest This technique is very popular online and is usually presented with claims like "puts you to sleep in two minutes". There is no controlled study behind those claims. What we do have: the general effects of slow breathing and of a long exhale are well demonstrated, and this technique contains both. So how it works looks reasonable. But "4-7-8 cures insomnia" is not a measured result. The numbers themselves — why seven, why eight — don't rest on any measurement either. They come from traditional teaching. An exhale done over six seconds instead of eight probably does the same job. We keep the technique in the app because many people look for it and how it works is understandable. But we don't write an inflated sentence about it. How to do it Lying down or sitting. Touch the tip of your tongue to the palate behind your upper teeth (that is the classic instruction; it isn't required). Breathe in through the nose for four seconds. Don't fill until you burst — just enough for an eight-second exhale. Hold for seven seconds. Don't lock the throat. Breathe out through the mouth for eight seconds, with the "ffff" sound. Let the sound last to the end. Shorter in the first session In the app the first session of this technique comes shortened: four in, four held, six out. The reason is that a seven-second hold feels harsh to someone who isn't used to it. Anyone who says "I'm experienced" doesn't get the shortening; the technique comes in full the first time. One exception: anyone over sixty-five or under thirteen gets the shortened version even if experienced. Common mistakes Making the inhale too deep. The most widespread mistake, and it causes a chain: too much air makes the hold harder and the exhale can't spread across eight seconds. Finishing the exhale in three or four seconds. Keep the "ffff" going to the end. If you can't, take in less on the inhale. Ignoring dizziness. In early sessions more than four cycles can make you dizzy. If it happens, stop. How the app measures it The exhale is through the mouth and audible, so it is easy to measure. The seven-second hold window is measured separately — a hold leak is the most common problem in this technique, because seven seconds is long. Who should take care For people who mark a tendency to dizziness, the app steers away from this technique. Long holds can be uncomfortable for people with blood pressure problems; shortening the length or choosing a technique without holds is better. Avoiding long holds in pregnancy is general advice.

b: Getting around the app
o: Which screen you reach from where. A map of the home screen, Profile, Settings and the Learn section.
g: There are four main stops in the app. All of them are one tap from the home screen. The home screen The Start button in the middle. Above it a line: a short pointer for the day, a new feature, or which interface level you are on. Below it the streak card: how many days you have kept going and your next milestone . Tap it and the calendar opens. Two icons at the top: Learn on the left, Profile on the right. The background changes with the day and the season. Light during the day, warm orange in the evening, dark and starry at night. Start → choosing a technique The technique list and the length slider . You pick a card and set the length; the button at the bottom starts a session with the technique and length you chose. If it is your first time with the technique, the tutorial comes in between. Learn Every technique explained. You can read them without doing a session: what each is good for, how it is done, the mistakes people make and why it works. Locked techniques appear here too — they don't have to be unlocked to be read about. Below them are three more sections: the Why does it work? cards, each with a Source link to the study behind it; a card on the Limits of slow breathing; and Safety and About . How we pick the sources is an article of its own . Profile A kind of control panel: Weekly summaries — what happened, week by week Programs — your running program, the catalogue and the history Streak — the calendar and milestones Session history — every session Achievements — earned and remaining Personal summary — the long view Settings If you have a program running, the Programs row says which day you are on. Settings Session: microphone, session rhythm haptics, sound cue, tap haptics, the hands-on round in tutorials, showing tutorials again. Appearance: light theme, dark theme or the system setting. The interface level is here too. Notification options: daily reminder, streak alert, technique-specific notifications, quiet hours, holiday mode , the daily cap, notification texts. Privacy: the anonymous sharing switches. Your intake answers : goal, experience, default length , usual time, age, health notes. All of them can be changed here. Your widgets , the version and deleting all your data are at the bottom. Screens that look locked Programs, the weekly summaries and the personal summary open after a certain point. While locked, the row still appears and tapping it tells you what is needed. When a screen unlocks, a short notice slides across the top of the home screen.

b: Getting the most out of the app
o: Two people use the same app and get very different results from it. The ten things that make the difference, and how to do each of them.
g: Opening the app, breathing for two minutes and closing it is a way of using it. But it is a small part of what the app can give you. Here is what makes the difference. 1. Actually fill in the intake You can skip it, but everything afterwards feeds on it: which technique gets suggested, how many minutes get suggested, how many sessions each lock will ask for, which warnings appear. Three answers matter most: your experience level (don't overstate it, don't undersell it), your health notes (mark them if you really have them) and your age . None of the three leaves your device. If your answer has changed since, update it: Profile → Settings → intake answers . 2. Short, and finished A finished two-minute session beats an abandoned six-minute one by every measure. Your completion rate affects both your score and the suggestions that follow. The length range the app suggests already takes this into account: if you have started abandoning sessions, the range shortens by itself. 3. Place the device properly This is where most of the value is lost. Twenty to thirty centimetres from your mouth and nose, microphone not covered. Propping it against something rather than laying it flat on a table makes a clear difference. If the measurement isn't right, the score and the suggestions become meaningless — everything the app can tell you rests on that measurement. 4. Stay quiet while the room is measured The three seconds at the start of a session set the threshold for the whole session. A sound during that window is taken for room noise, and you then get listened to with the wrong threshold for the rest of the session. 5. Read the whole report, at least for the first few weeks The score at the top is the least informative part. The real information is under Detailed report : which component is low, which measurement is borderline. If your interface level is Simple, the report shrinks to a single sentence. While you are still learning, Standard or Advanced is more useful. 6. Don't hop between techniques — settle into one Trying a different technique every day is fun, but you make no progress in any of them. The app keeps separate statistics per technique: keep to the same one for a few weeks and both your score and your suggested length settle for that technique. Pick one technique, stay with it for two weeks, then change. 7. Set up a program A pile of single sessions doesn't add up to a program. A program tracks doing the same technique for the same length every day, and at the end it lays out day by day what happened. The first program is twenty-eight days, five minutes a day — and those five minutes aren't an arbitrary number; that is the length used in the study the program is based on. 8. Set the reminder to suit you The most common reason for missing a day is forgetting. But a reminder set at the wrong time is no use either: a notification you dismiss at the same time every day is noise, not a habit. You can give a separate time to each day of the week. Mornings on weekdays, midday at the weekend, say. 9. Move to your own pace The five and a half seconds of Coherent Breathing is an average. Measuring your own resonance pace takes a few minutes, and after that every Coherent session runs at a pace that suits you. If you are going to use the app regularly, this is the single highest-return thing you can do. 10. Go back to your own data Once a month, look at the weekly summaries and the personal summary. Which time of day goes better for you, which technique you are improving in, which days you miss — it is all written there. Without that information, building a habit means working from guesswork. And one thing not to do Don't make the score the goal. The score measures how closely you followed the pace on screen, not whether the breathing did you good. Forcing your breath for a higher score — pushing the exhale, raising its volume — both spoils the technique and lowers the score anyway. What the app measures is a tool. The point is how you feel after the session.

b: History, summaries and achievements
o: Session history, the weekly summary, the personal summary and achievements. What each one shows and when it opens.
g: Everything your sessions add up to shows in four separate places. All of them are reached from Profile . Session history A list of every session you have done: date, technique, length and score. Tap a session and that day's report opens — with its measurements, exactly as you saw it at the time. This is the most direct way to see whether you are improving in a particular technique. Weekly summaries The weeks sit side by side. For each week you get how many sessions, how many minutes, the average score, and what changed against the week before. Tap a week and its detail opens: which techniques you did, which days were completed, how your scores moved. A week that went well can be kept at the top of the list with Pin to top , which makes comparing later weeks easier. You unpin it from the same place. If you want the week's summary as a notification on Sunday evening, that option is in Notification options . The weekly summaries open after a certain point. While locked, they tell you what is needed. The personal summary A longer view drawn from your whole session history, section by section: Observations — a few sentences drawn from your data: the technique you do most, the one you are best at, the time of day that goes better for you. Your session habits — how often, how long and at what time of day you practise. Suggestions for you — advice drawn from what keeps coming back in your measurements. Mistakes you make often — which short note came up most during your sessions. The thing to work on is usually written here. Component averages — the long-run average of the measurements behind the score . Whichever one stays low shows up here. Your average measurements — the averages of numbers like exhale length and rhythm match. At the bottom, Technical values opens on the Advanced interface: the averages of raw numbers like the noise floor and the exhale peak level. This screen also opens once you have built up enough sessions. Achievements There are dozens of achievements: to do with trying techniques, keeping it up, scores and programs. The ones you have earned are in colour, the ones you haven't are faded, and each says what it needs. The notification that tells you when you are close to an achievement is optional: Notification options → Tell me when an achievement is close . Achievements aren't a list of targets; they are a record of what you did, to look back on. The interface level changes this too All three summary screens get simpler or fuller depending on your interface level : On Simple , they say what you did. On Standard , how it went. On Advanced , why it went that way. At the Simple level the screen doesn't go empty; only the weight of interpretation drops. If you want more, change it under Settings → Interface . Where your data is All of this sits on your device. If iCloud is on it syncs in your own account — so when you sign in on another device your history is there. We have no developer access to that area.

b: How a session is scored
o: The number out of a hundred is a weighted average of several separate measurements. How much weight each carries, why, and what the score doesn't tell you.
g: The number on screen when a session ends doesn't measure one thing. There are several separate measurements, each with its own weight, and on top of that a multiplier that affects them all. The measurements Rhythm match. The gap between the moment the circle starts shrinking and the moment your exhale starts. Measured separately for each cycle, then averaged. This is the heaviest component, because it is the app's real job: settling your breath into a pace. Exhales heard. How many of your target exhales were heard, and how many of those were genuinely near the target. Both are measured, because looking at the first alone would mislead: someone breathing out at random intervals would "catch" every target. An average that rewards both is taken: if one is low, the result comes out low. Exhale length. How close the exhale is to the target length. Against a three-second target, breathing out for two seconds counts as the same amount of deviation as five. Inhale and inhale length. The inhale is far quieter than the exhale, so it is measured separately with lower thresholds . Not hearing the inhale at all doesn't sink the score by itself: some people's nasal inhale really is silent. Breath volume. How far the exhale rises above the noise floor . Both too quiet and too loud are penalised. Too loud isn't a good sign: it means forcing the breath, pushing instead of letting go. Exhale smoothness. How much the sound level varies through the exhale. A steady "ffff" gives a small deviation; a broken or rasping exhale gives a large one. Cycle consistency. How much the cycles resemble one another. One clean cycle among scattered ones brings this down. Holds and hold length. In techniques with a hold phase, whether a sound was heard in that window — if it was, air escaped — and whether the hold lasted as long as it should. Completion. How much of the session you did. Which measurements count depends on the technique : a technique without holds has no hold components at all, and if the inhale could not be measured the inhale components drop out. The Humming Bee adds a hum component. The weights of whatever remains are shared out again among themselves. The weights and the rhythm multiplier The weights are fixed: rhythm match takes the largest share, followed by exhales heard and exhale length, with the inhale-related components carrying the smallest share. On top of the weighted average there is one more multiplier. If most of the exhales fell outside the target, the whole score is lowered proportionally: a session that never caught the rhythm can get at most half marks even if its other measurements are good. The reason is simple — a well-formed breath outside the circle is a well-formed breath, but not that session's breath. {{puan-panosu}} Above ninety-three is written as a hundred When the raw score passes ninety-three, the screen shows a hundred. That is a decision about presentation: writing ninety-six for someone who scored ninety-six was belittling a session that was, in fact, close to flawless. There is one exception. If any component has fallen below seventy, no rounding happens and the real score is written. The reason is consistency: a session where every exhale lasted half the target isn't a "hundred" even if the average comes out high. Writing "your exhales are short" in one part of the report while a hundred sits at the top would be the app contradicting itself. What the score doesn't tell you This number is not a measure of health. It doesn't measure whether your breathing is "correct", whether the exercise did you good, or whether you relaxed. The only thing it measures is how closely you followed the pace on screen. It is possible to get a low score and feel very good. It is possible to get a high score and feel nothing. Both are normal — the number is a feedback tool, not a grade. There is also the microphone's limit: the app measures the sound of your breath, not the breath itself. Someone who breathes out very quietly, sits far from the microphone or is in a noisy room can score lower than what they actually did. The technical measurements in the report exist so you can see this: the noise floor and the exhale peak level are written there.

b: What your suggestions depend on
o: The suggested technique and the suggested length aren't fixed. Your intake answers, your past sessions, the time of day, and the places where these intersect.
g: Two people opening the app don't see the same screen. Both the order of the techniques and the length range marked on the slider are built for the person. Here is what gets looked at. The suggested length is a range, not a number The lit band above the slider means "for this session, your range is here". The middle of the range starts from a base length and shifts with seven separate factors. The base length. Usually the length you gave in the intake . But in some techniques it comes not from your answer but from the length applied in the studies — twenty-seven cycles in Left and Right Nostril Breathing , for instance. The reason: in these techniques, going below the dose isn't "doing a bit less", it is not doing the thing that was measured. Experience. For a beginner the range shortens; for an experienced person it lengthens. Overall and recent performance. If your recent sessions went well the range lengthens; if you struggled it shortens. Your overall average and the average of your last five sessions are worked out separately and weighed together. The recent ones count for more. Performance in the same technique. Overall performance and performance in that technique are kept apart. The same person can finish coherent comfortably and abandon 4-7-8 . Completion rate. Sessions you abandon shorten the range. A short session finished beats a long one abandoned. Time of day. Late in the day the range shortens: a ten-minute session at midnight isn't realistic. Streak. For someone on a running streak the range lengthens a little. If a program is running, none of this applies: the length becomes the program's daily length and is locked. The order of the techniques The order of the cards isn't fixed either. Your goal is the main determinant: calm, focus, sleep, energy or "just trying it". The time of day sits on top of that — the energizing breath moves up in the morning and down at night. Then what you have already done today comes in. A technique done today drops back , and something else is suggested instead. A technique you have done often in the last two weeks moves down a little, and one you have neglected moves up a little. The technique's difficulty against your experience, your score in it and your completion rate all feed into the order too. If you have a program running and haven't done that day's session, the program's technique goes to the top. None of these is strong enough to jump a level. A technique your health notes steer you away from always stays at the bottom; no contribution can lift it. Where your answers change each other This is the most interesting part. The intake answers don't work one by one — they intersect. Age × experience. The first session of a technique comes softened: in 4-7-8 the hold is four seconds instead of seven; in Kapalabhati a single slow round. Anyone who says "I'm experienced" doesn't get this, and the technique comes in full the first time. But age takes that exemption back: someone over sixty-five starts with a soft first session even if experienced. Age × interface. Over sixty-five, the suggested interface level is Simple. That is why the age question comes before the interface question — coming after, it couldn't have affected the suggestion. Age × goal. For someone over sixty-five who says "for energy", the technique that unlocks isn't the Energizing Breath but Right Nostril. The goal stays the same; the technique that serves it changes. Health × goal. The same logic runs for health notes. If someone marks a heart condition and says "for energy", unlocking the Energizing Breath and putting a warning next to it would have the app contradicting itself. There is an ordered list for each goal, and the first technique not steered against is the one that opens. Your experience level sets how many sessions the locks ask for, and the score of your introductory exercise raises or lowers that. So the answers you gave on the first day are still affecting which technique opens when, months later. All of it on the device None of the intake answers is sent anywhere. Age, health notes, goal, experience — all of it stays on the device and is used only to feed these calculations. You can change them in Settings whenever you like.

b: How the microphone hears your breath
o: If audio isn't recorded, how does the app measure your breath? The noise floor, a threshold that moves with the room, and how the start and end of an exhale are found.
g: The app doesn't record audio. The stream from the microphone is never written to disk; every twenty milliseconds the sound level at that instant is worked out, and only that number is kept. So what the app holds isn't an audio file but a series of numbers: a line that rises and falls. Every measurement is made from that line. Silence is measured first There is a three-second listen at the start of a session. In that time the room's noise floor is measured: the hum of the fridge, traffic outside, the device's own electronic noise. It isn't an average — it looks at the quietest moments of those three seconds. The reason: putting the phone down on a table during calibration, or someone coughing, pulls the average up and leaves the threshold wrong for the whole session. In one real recording this caused a fourteen-decibel error. The floor is updated during the session too. If the room goes quieter the threshold comes down; if noise rises it goes up — but only within limits, otherwise the app would deafen itself in a noisy room. The threshold isn't absolute, it is relative to the floor For a sound to count as an "exhale" it doesn't have to pass a particular decibel level. It has to rise a certain amount above the floor . In a quiet room that threshold is low; in a noisy café it is high. How far above the floor depends on the technique. A breath out through the mouth (extended exhale, pursed lip) comes out loud. A calm breath out through the nose (coherent, box) is much lower. A breath through a single nostril is the lowest of all. Every technique is listened to with its own threshold; holding them all to the same bar would make the nasal techniques inaudible. The start and end of an exhale The raw sound level is too jittery to use directly. It is smoothed first — each new measurement is blended with the one before, so a single click doesn't turn into an exhale. The exhale begins when the smoothed line crosses the threshold. For it to end, either of two conditions is enough: the line drops below the threshold and stays there for a third of a second, or it falls a certain amount from the exhale's own peak. Without the second condition, an audible inhale would extend the exhale and two breaths would be measured as one. Very short events are discarded. For that the raw measurement is used rather than the smoothed line: smoothing stretches a short click and makes it look longer than it was. The quiet room and the tablet problem Thresholds being relative to the floor works in most cases, but it has a trap: if the floor really is very low, the relative threshold becomes over-sensitive and every creak in the room can count as an exhale. So there is a lower bound on how far the floor can go. That bound was too high for a while. In one tablet recording the real noise floor measured far lower; because the bound assumed the floor was higher than it was, the exhale's margin melted away and nothing was heard at all. Someone breathing out a hand's width from the tablet was being told to "bring the device closer". The bound was rescanned against twenty-one real recordings and lowered: the number of exhales caught went up and the number of false detections didn't change. Decisions like this are made from the recordings we have, not from guesswork — that is the only job audio sample sharing does. Fast breathing is a separate job This method has a limit: telling that an exhale has ended needs a short silence afterwards. In a technique breathing out faster than once a second, that silence never appears. So Kapalabhati is measured a different way. Rather than trying to separate the exhales one by one, the app counts the moments when the sound line peaks and looks at how regular the gaps are. The counter waits for the line to fall below the threshold after a peak closes — without that condition it was counting every exhale twice.

b: How we read the evidence
o: Most breathing studies are small, uncontrolled and short. What each sentence in the app rests on, and what we deliberately don't write.
g: Most of the sentences you read online about breathing exercises claim more than the study behind them says. In the app and on this site we try not to do that. Here is how we decide. Three separate levels of confidence The things that can be said about a technique aren't equally solid. We divide them roughly into three. A measured physiological effect. Heart rate variability increasing at close to six breaths a minute, for instance. Repeated, understandable in how it works, measured with instruments. We write this directly. A result seen in a controlled study. The physiological sigh coming out ahead of other methods in mood measures in a one-month study , for instance. There is a comparison group and a defined dose. We write this naming the study : "in this study, under these conditions, this was seen." What tradition says. The cooling breath cooling the body, Kapalabhati cleansing, and so on. We either don't write these at all, or write them while saying they belong to tradition. The common problems of breathing research Small participant numbers. Studies of twenty or thirty people are common. At that size a chance result comes easily. Weak control groups. A comparison of "a group doing breathing exercises against a group doing nothing" may be measuring the effect of doing something , not of the breathing. Good studies use an active comparison group. It can't be blinded. In drug trials the person doesn't know which group they are in. In a breathing exercise they do. Separating out the expectation effect is very hard for that reason. Self-reported measures. "I felt calmer" is valuable data but it isn't a number measured with an instrument. Undefined dose. Many studies don't state clearly how many minutes, how many days, or at what pace. A study that doesn't say can't be turned into an app. What that means in the app Cooling Breath. Tradition calls it "cooling". In Telles and colleagues' 2020 study body temperature was measured and did not drop. The app says so plainly; the store description never claims "it cools the body" either, only describing the sensation of coolness in the mouth — that sensation is real, the cooling isn't the thing that was measured. Left and Right Nostril Breathing. The source studies measure single-nostril practice and their participant numbers are small. The text in the app says this openly, along with the weakness of the evidence and the fact that the second values aren't found in the sources. Right Nostril and the night. There are findings that right nostril breathing increases alertness, but they are weak. So the technique isn't removed from the suggestions at night; only a soft note is added. In the Energizing Breath the note is firmer, because the evidence there is stronger. Dose. In Left and Right Nostril, the suggested length comes not from the person's answers but from the length applied in the studies. The reason: in these techniques, going below the dose isn't "doing a bit less", it is not doing the thing that was measured. Sentences we don't write Sentences of this kind are deliberately absent from the app and the site: "cures anxiety", "lowers blood pressure", "strengthens your immune system", "treats insomnia", "removes toxins". Some of them may be true. But they aren't things the evidence in hand lets us say, and it isn't right for an app to make medical promises to its users. Soluklan is a relaxation and focus exercise app. It doesn't diagnose, it doesn't treat, and it doesn't take the place of a doctor's advice. Where we get it wrong This approach isn't flawless. When we couldn't find a technique's threshold values in the sources, we have taken them over from similar techniques. Some numbers — how many seconds in, how many out — come from traditional teaching and have no measured counterpart. In places like that the app's own text says so. When we don't know something, the sentence we write is "we don't know". Source links in the articles Every sentence resting on a study has that study's address under it. Most go to a PubMed record or the publisher's full-text page — you can look for yourself and compare it with what we wrote. Where we couldn't verify a source's full record, we put a search link instead of a direct one. We would rather send you to a search than to the wrong study.

b: Humming Bee Breath
o: Mouth closed, ten seconds of "mmm". The only technique in the app where the sound itself is measured: the microphone isn't looking for a quiet breath, it is looking for a vibration.
g: Breathe in through the nose for four seconds. Close your lips, teeth slightly apart. Breathe out over ten seconds with an "mmm" sound, like a bee humming. Its Sanskrit name is Bhramari, meaning "honeybee". What it is good for It has two sides. The mechanical side. The hum lengthens and smooths the exhale by itself. A ten-second exhale is hard to do silently and easy to do with a sound — the sound holds the pace of the exhale steady on its own. So this technique is really an exercise in a long, even exhale. The vibration side. The hum creates vibration in the nasal and facial cavities. That vibration has been measured to increase the release of nitric oxide in the nasal cavity. Nitric oxide's role in the airways and circulation is known, but what the increase produced by humming means in daily life is unclear. So "humming raises nitric oxide" is a correct sentence; "the humming bee breath strengthens your immune system" is not. How to do it Sit comfortably. Breathe in through the nose for four seconds. Close your lips, part your teeth slightly, relax your jaw. Breathe out through the nose over ten seconds with an "mmm" sound. Keep the sound soft and in one piece . It doesn't have to be loud; continuous is enough. If you close your ears lightly with your fingers, the vibration comes through more strongly. Common mistakes Letting the sound break up. It should be one piece at an even volume. A broken sound both splits the exhale and lowers the measurement. Squeezing the throat. The sound should come from vibration in the nose, not from straining the larynx. If your throat gets tired, you are pushing too hard. Trying to carry on when the breath runs out. When the air is gone, end the sound and take a calm breath in. How the app measures it This is the only technique in the app where the microphone looks at the quality of the sound, not just its level. A hum is a continuous, low sound. The sound of breath is an irregular rustle. The app measures how much of the exhale consists of that continuous sound and shows a separate "hum" component in the report. In practice that means: breathing out quietly for a long time doesn't earn full marks in this technique. Without the sound, the exhale doesn't count.
