Who should take care If you have an ear infection or an eardrum problem, skip the part where you cover your ears. No other known risk. Source Weitzberg & Lundberg (2002), American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine — nitric oxide in the nasal cavity rises fifteen-fold during humming. PubMed

b: Making the interface simpler or fuller
o: Simple, Standard and Advanced. What changes across the three levels, who each one suits, and how to switch.
g: You choose how much information the app shows. There are three levels, and the difference is only in what you see: no feature is switched off and no measurement stops. Simple On the home screen, just Start and your streak. Tutorials are short. In the session report , a score and a single sentence. The summary screens get simpler too: they say what you did, and the weight of interpretation drops. Who it suits: people who want the app purely as a breathing exercise, people who don't want to deal with numbers, and older users. Standard The balanced one. Tutorials, the hands-on round, the detailed report, achievements and summaries. In the report, measurements and suggestions appear next to your score, and Detailed report takes you deeper. This is the one suggested for most people. Advanced Everything open. All the technical lines in the report (inhale level, exhale peak level, variation within the exhale), every section of the summary screens, and — under the length slider — why the range is where it is . Who it suits: people who enjoy reading measurements, and people who want to track what is changing in their breathing. How to change it Profile → Settings → Interface. It changes instantly, nothing is lost, and you can go back whenever you like. You are asked in the intake too. If you are over sixty-five, Simple comes pre-selected there — that is a suggestion; pick whatever you want. If you forget which one you're on Above the Start button on the home screen there is a line telling you which level you are on: it reminds someone on Simple that they can ask for more, and someone on Advanced that they can step down if it feels crowded. The look is a separate thing Don't confuse the interface level with Appearance . Appearance is the light theme, dark theme or follow-the-system option — a separate row, also in Settings. The background also changes with the day and the season: light during the day, warm orange in the evening, dark and starry at night. Snow in winter, leaves in spring. Sunrise and sunset are worked out on your device; no location data is used.

b: Kapalabhati
o: Fast, forceful exhales from the abdominal muscles. The one stimulating advanced technique in the app, the one with the longest list of who shouldn't do it, and the one the microphone measures a different way.
g: Pull your belly in and breathe out through the nose, short and forceful. Don't think about the inhale — it comes by itself when the belly relaxes. Repeat this faster than once a second. This technique isn't like the others. It doesn't calm, it stimulates . You choose rounds rather than a length. And it is the technique in the app to approach most carefully. The warning first Don't do this technique if any of the following applies: high blood pressure, a heart condition, epilepsy, pregnancy, recent surgery, a hernia, or recent eye surgery. These aren't advisories built on weak evidence; they are warnings repeated consistently in traditional teaching and in clinical sources. Fast, forceful exhales raise the pressure inside the abdomen and can cause sudden swings in blood pressure. The app doesn't hide this technique from anyone who marks a health note in the intake , but it does steer away from it: the card drops to the bottom, the warning becomes firmer, and the upper limit on rounds drops. If you feel dizzy, tingling, dimmed vision or ringing in the ears, stop immediately and go back to normal breathing. These aren't symptoms to push through. What it is good for Its name means "shining skull" and it is traditionally counted as a cleansing practice. The measurable side is its stimulating effect. Studies by Telles and colleagues report increased alertness and better performance on some cognitive tasks after fast-breathing practices. Think of it like coffee: a short-lived arousal. That is why it is done during the day and on an empty stomach , not before bed. The other effects described in tradition — clearing the lungs, regulating digestion, "releasing toxins" — have no measured counterpart. The app doesn't write them. What a round is In the other techniques you pick a length; here you pick rounds . One round is twenty-five breaths done one after another, followed by half a minute of normal breathing. The break is part of the round, not a rest. It is needed for the body to come back to itself after fast breathing. The first session of the technique comes as a single round, twenty breaths, at one per second — slower than normal and without the break. In later sessions the pace rises to one and a half per second and you can choose from one to five rounds. It doesn't go to two per second: the risk of dizziness rises, and the microphone goes completely blind at that pace. How to do it Sit upright, shoulders loose. Put a hand on your belly — you'll feel the movement. Take a normal breath in through the nose; don't fill your lungs completely. Pull your belly sharply in and breathe out through the nose, short and forceful. Release the belly and let the inhale come by itself. Repeat rhythmically. The movement must come from the belly . If your shoulders are moving, you are breathing out from the chest. Why the tutorial's try-out is slow The tutorials in the app include a hands-on round. In this technique the try-out isn't the same as the session: a normal inhale first, then three slow exhales. The reason is simple. Giving someone who has never done it twenty-five fast pumps in a row isn't teaching. This technique is already the repetition of a single movement: learn the pump and you have learned the technique; speed comes afterwards. That is the order in yoga teaching too. There is a second reason: the microphone can't separate individual exhales at that pace, so a fast try-out couldn't have been measured either. How the app measures it In the other techniques, telling that an exhale has ended needs a short silence afterwards. At one and a half breaths a second, that silence never appears. So Kapalabhati is measured with a separate counter. Rather than trying to separate the exhales one by one, the app counts the moments when the sound line peaks and looks at how regular the gaps between them are. The report's measurement follows from that: how many breaths were counted, what fraction of the expected number that is, and how regular the rhythm was. Sources Telles et al. (2011), Perceptual and Motor Skills — the effect of kapalabhati on perception and attention, compared with breath awareness. PubMed Telles et al. (2015), Medical Science Monitor Basic Research — metabolic and respiratory changes measured during and after the practice: the numerical counterpart of the technique's stimulating side. PubMed For who shouldn't do it: the list repeated across Saraswati's Asana Pranayama Mudra Bandha and yoga therapy sources. It rests not on a single study but on the warnings those sources hold in common.

b: Managing your data
o: What is kept where, what syncs between devices, the sharing options, and deleting everything.
g: Here is where everything the app keeps actually lives, and what you can control. Data that stays on your device Your session summaries (date, technique, length, score, report), your intake answers , your settings and your notification preferences are stored on your device. If iCloud is on, your session history syncs in your own iCloud account . So when you sign in on another device your history is there. We have no developer access to that area — it sits on Apple's infrastructure, in your account. Your settings and intake answers sync in the same account, so a new device sets itself up the way you left it. Audio Audio is not recorded. The microphone runs only during a session and only the instant sound level is worked out from it. No audio file is written to disk. The one exception is the audio sample permission below — if you haven't turned it on, audio is never recorded in any session. Optional sharing There are three separate switches under Settings → Privacy. All of them start off and each is asked about separately. Anonymous usage summary. A randomly generated identifier, the date and time, the technique, the length, the score, whether it was completed, whether the microphone was used, the app version and the technical values from the report. Your name, email address, location, device identifier and health answers are never sent. Audio sample. Now and then the audio of a session is sent in compressed form. Its only purpose is to measure the accuracy of breath detection. The file that is sent is deleted from your device. This option appears only if you turned the usage summary on, and is never shown to anyone who says they are under thirteen. Heart rate summary. Only for sessions done with an Apple Watch, and only with separate permission. All of these can be turned off whenever you like. If you turn audio sharing off, any pending audio files are deleted too. We have written a separate article on what happens to the records you share after they reach us. The question that comes up now and then If you turned anonymous sharing on, a short question may appear at the end of a session now and then: a score out of ten, followed by one more question. Both can be skipped. Along with the score, the text you write is sent too — answer knowing that, and don't put anything identifying in the box. The full list of what is sent is in what we do with the data you share . If you skip it, the app doesn't ask again for a while, and that wait grows with each skip. After a few skips it stops asking altogether. You are also asked once when you finish or abandon a program. Deleting everything At the bottom of the settings is Delete all your data? . If you confirm, all the session history, profile and settings on the device are deleted, and the app starts again from the intake. For the iCloud copy you need to use Apple's iCloud settings. If you want records you shared anonymously deleted as well, writing to the support address is enough. If you delete the app The data on the device is deleted. The iCloud copy stays for a while under Apple's rules; if you reinstall the app, your history comes back.

b: How the thresholds are measured against real recordings
o: What counts as an "exhale" isn't decided by guesswork but from real audio samples sent by users. How that work runs.
g: For the app to count a sound as an exhale, that sound has to be a certain amount above the room's silence. So where does that "certain amount" come from? From a guess at first. From measurement afterwards. Why it starts with a guess When a new technique is added, we don't have a single recording of it. The threshold is taken over from similar techniques: for a technique breathed out through the mouth, the value of another mouth technique in the same family; for a nasal one, the nasal family's. That guess is usually roughly right but not exact. The app's text doesn't hide it — where a value has no source, it says "initial values, to be measured when data arrives". How the measurement is done From users who turn on anonymous sharing and audio sample sharing, the audio of a session arrives now and then. With it comes that session's report and raw timing: at which seconds the target exhales were expected, at which moments the app detected an exhale, and what the noise floor was. With those two together the measurement becomes possible. The audio file is run through the app's own detection code — the same code, the same arithmetic — but with the threshold changed. Then the question: at which threshold were how many target exhales caught, and how many false detections occurred? The result is a table: threshold exhales caught extra events current 32/61 74 slightly lower 35/61 74 lower still 35/61 74 If catches rise and false detections don't, the threshold is lowered. If both rise, it is left alone. A real example The app has a lower bound on how far the noise floor can go: it stops the thresholds becoming over-sensitive in very quiet rooms. In one tablet recording the real noise floor measured far below that bound. Because the bound assumed the floor was higher than it was, the exhale's margin melted away and nothing was heard — someone breathing out a hand's width from the tablet was being told to "bring the device closer". It was scanned against twenty-one real recordings and the bound was lowered: the number of exhales caught went up, the number of false detections didn't change. That session alone went from zero out of four to two out of four. A correction like this can't be found by guesswork. Without the recording we wouldn't even have known the problem existed. This is the only job audio sample sharing does The audio that is sent is listened to for this and nothing else: measuring the accuracy of breath detection. It isn't used for any other purpose, isn't given to third parties, and is deleted from your device once sent. If it is off, audio is never recorded in any session. The app works completely without this permission — new techniques' thresholds just stay guesses for longer. Still unmeasured At the time of writing, some techniques' thresholds are still running on their initial values: not enough recordings have built up. As they do, the same scan is run again and the values are updated. So the app's measurement accuracy grows along with the people using it.

b: There is no third-party code in the app
o: Ad network, analytics tool, crash reporter, ready-made interface library — none of them. What that means and what it costs.
g: Most iOS apps carry dozens of third-party packages inside them: analytics tools, ad networks, crash reporters, ready-made interface libraries. Soluklan has none of these. What isn't there No ad network. No advertising is shown in the app and no advertising identifier is read. No analytics tool. There is no tool tracking which screen you opened how many times, which button you tapped, or how long you stayed in the app. No crash reporter. If the app crashes, no automatic report comes to us. Information arrives only through Apple's own system, to the extent you allow it in your device settings. No ready-made libraries. The interface, the audio processing, the drawings, the animations — all written with Apple's own frameworks. What is there There are two places the app uses the network, and both are Apple's infrastructure: iCloud. Your session history syncs in your own account. We have no developer access to that area. Anonymous sharing. If you turned it on, session summaries come through — and, if you gave separate permission, an audio sample now and then. These sit on Apple's CloudKit infrastructure. Beyond these the app connects to no server at all. Even notifications are scheduled on the device: we have no server for sending notifications. What it costs This choice has a price, and we won't hide it. Less information. We don't know which feature gets used, where people get stuck, or on which screen they give up. Session summaries from users who turn on anonymous sharing are the only data we have. Slower bug-finding. When a crash happens, we only learn about it if someone tells us or if we see it in Apple's reports. More work. What a ready-made library would do in a day takes several days to write. Why it is still this way The app's job is to listen to your breath. The sound of a breath is data passing through a microphone, and putting third-party packages into an app that holds that data means trusting what those packages do. If the privacy policy says "no ads, no tracking, no third-party analytics", that has to have a counterpart on the code side. Writing the sentence is easy; keeping the sentence true is a matter of not adding packages. How to check for yourself What data an app collects is written on its privacy label in the App Store. And if you turn on iOS's Settings → Privacy & Security → App Privacy Report , you can see on your own device which app connected to which domains.

b: Ocean Breath
o: The rustle of air passing through your throat. A silent inhale, an exhale like a seashell. Getting the sound right is the technique itself.
g: Breathe in quietly through the nose for four seconds. Narrow your throat very slightly and breathe out through the nose over six seconds — letting out a soft rustle like a seashell. Its Sanskrit name is Ujjayi. It is the breath you hear about most in yoga classes. Where the sound comes from Not from the vocal cords. Narrowing the air passage at the back of the throat very slightly makes the air rub as it passes, and that rustle is the result. The easiest way to find it: open your mouth and breathe out onto your palm with a "haaa", as if fogging a window. What is happening in your throat at that moment is the right thing. Then close your mouth without interrupting the breath — the sound softens but continues. The tutorial in the app follows exactly this order. What it is good for That slight narrowing slows the exhale by itself. You get a long exhale without forcing it. Its second job, and perhaps its real one, is about attention: a continuous sound leaves a marker you can return to when your mind drifts. That is also why it is so widespread in yoga classes — it makes following the breath easier while moving. No sound on the inhale The classical texts ask for sound on both the inhale and the exhale. In the app we ask for it only on the exhale. The reason is measurement: adding sound to the inhale was found to add nothing and to raise heart rate. Leaving the inhale free makes the technique both easier and better working. How to do it Sit upright. Breathe in quietly through the nose for four seconds — do nothing on the inhale . Narrow your throat very slightly and breathe out through the nose over six seconds. The sound should be no louder than a whisper: someone next to you hears it, someone two metres away doesn't. Common mistakes Squeezing the throat. The most widespread mistake. Narrowing doesn't mean using muscle — the air should rub by itself. If your throat hurts, you are pushing too hard; let it go. Humming. This technique isn't "mmm", that is the Humming Bee Breath. The sound here is the rustle of air. Trying to make a sound on the inhale too. The inhale is free. How the app measures it Because the exhale is audible, this is one of the easier techniques to measure. The thresholds are set accordingly. What is looked at most is the smoothness of the exhale : the rustle should hold an even volume from start to finish. If the sound cuts out or wavers, there is tension in the throat or the breath is running short. The measurement was tuned once against real recordings: the first values were estimates, and the thresholds were checked when test data arrived. Who should take care If your throat is sore or irritated, don't do this technique. Forcing to produce a sound gains you nothing — a forced Ocean Breath isn't Ocean Breath. Sources Hatha Yoga Pradipika (15th century, chapter 2, verses 51-53) — the classical description of the technique. For studies comparing different forms of slow yogic breathing: search PubMed . The app's decision to leave the inhale silent rests on those comparisons.

b: The Physiological Sigh
o: Two inhales stacked, then one long exhale. The technique with the best controlled study among short breathing exercises. It is also the program's technique.
g: Breathe in through the nose, add a second short inhale on top before your lungs are full, then breathe out through the mouth, long and slow. One cycle takes about ten seconds. This is what a sigh actually is: the body already does it by itself, in sleep and during the day, minutes apart. The technique is nothing more than repeating that movement deliberately. Why two inhales Some of the air sacs inside the lung stay collapsed during ordinary breathing. The second short inhale, stacked on the first, opens them. That is why the second inhale must be short and must complete the first — it isn't a separate breath, it is the continuation of the same one. The long exhale is part of it too: a long, free exhale increases the amount of carbon dioxide released and brings the body's calming side forward. Where the evidence stands Among the techniques in the app, this is the one with the best controlled study . In work published by Balban and colleagues in Cell Reports Medicine in 2023, three different breathing exercises and mindfulness meditation were compared, done five minutes a day for a month. The physiological sigh came out ahead of the others in mood measures and in the drop in breathing rate. What makes that study matter: there is a comparison group, the duration is defined and the dose is defined. Most breathing studies have none of these. It has limits too. Participants numbered around a hundred, the period was one month, and the measures were mostly self-reported. "Doing it five minutes a day for a month showed improvement in mood measures" is a correct sentence; "the sigh takes anxiety away" does not come from that study. The program in the app comes from this study The first program in the Programs section follows that study's practice exactly: twenty-eight days, five minutes a day . The length slider is open and anyone can change it — but the suggested value isn't arbitrary, it is the dose that was measured. That is why we don't shorten the program's daily length per person. Going below the dose isn't "doing a bit less", it is not doing the thing that was measured. How to do it Sit upright. Take a normal breath in through the nose — don't fill your lungs completely , about three-quarters. Then add a short, sharp inhale on top. This second inhale lasts about a second and a half, clearly shorter than the first. Your lungs are now full. Breathe out through the mouth, long and slow. About six seconds, lips slightly parted. Let the exhale go; don't push it. There is no hold. Common mistakes Filling the lungs completely on the first inhale. The most common mistake. Fill completely and there is no room for the second inhale, and the technique loses its point. Making the second inhale long. If the second inhale is the same length as the first, you have taken two separate breaths, not one stacked on another. Cutting the exhale short. The exhale should be longer than the inhale. Cutting it short takes away most of the effect. How the app measures it The exhale is through the mouth so the sound is strong, and the thresholds match. The two inhales are measured separately: because the second is short and light, its threshold is lower still. The report shows the second inhale on its own line. If it wasn't heard, the reason is usually the same one: the lungs were filled completely on the first inhale and there was no room for the second. Who should take care It is one of the gentlest techniques in the app and doesn't even include a brief hold. Even so, two stacked inhales is an unfamiliar movement: mild dizziness is possible in the first sessions. If it happens, stop, take a few normal breaths, then carry on. Source Balban et al. (2023), Cell Reports Medicine — "Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal". Full text

b: Pursed Lip Breathing
o: Three seconds in through the nose, six seconds out through pursed lips. The core technique taught in pulmonary rehabilitation and the one most recommended for breathlessness.
g: Breathe in through the nose for three seconds. Purse your lips as if about to whistle. Breathe out slowly over six seconds. This technique comes from somewhere different from the others: not from relaxation practice but from pulmonary rehabilitation . What it is good for Pursed lips create a small resistance on the exhale. That resistance keeps the pressure inside the airways slightly raised until the end of the exhale. Why that matters: in some lung conditions the small airways close early during the exhale and part of the air gets trapped inside. The next inhale arrives at a lung that is already full, and the feeling of breathlessness follows. The resistance helps hold those airways open to the end of the exhale. This is one of the clearest mechanical rationales among breathing techniques. The effect isn't a feeling; it is about the physics of airflow. Where the evidence stands In people with COPD it is relatively well shown to reduce the sensation of breathlessness and to lower the breathing rate; it is a standard part of pulmonary rehabilitation programmes. There is less research on its effect in healthy people. That it lowers the breathing rate and lengthens the exhale is certain — those follow from the definition of the technique. The app is not a medical tool and doesn't offer this technique as a treatment. For anyone with a respiratory condition the right address is their doctor and a respiratory physiotherapist. How to do it Relax your shoulders. Breathe in through the nose for three seconds — the inhale is always through the nose . Purse your lips as if to whistle, but don't clench them. Breathe out slowly through the pursed lips over six seconds. Let the air leave like a thin line. Don't force it, don't push the last of the air out. Common mistakes Puffing the cheeks. If your cheeks puff, the pressure stays in your mouth and doesn't reach the airways. Keep the cheeks loose. Emptying by force. Pushing out the air at the end of the exhale works against the point of the technique: pushing closes the airways early. Breathing in through the mouth. The inhale is through the nose. Through the mouth, the air isn't filtered or moistened. How the app measures it Because the exhale is through the mouth and against resistance, the sound is pronounced. The thresholds are the same as for the family of mouth-exhale techniques. What the measurement looks at most is the smoothness of the exhale : a steady breath through pursed lips shows very little variation in sound level. A broken or falling sound shows the exhale is being strained. Who should take care This is one of the gentlest techniques in the app and doesn't even include a hold. It is suitable for someone experiencing breathlessness too — it was developed for exactly those situations. Even so, if discomfort increases, stop.

b: Reading your session report
o: What every line in the report means, and what to do about a measurement that came out low.
g: The screen that arrives when a session ends has a score at the top and a few sentences under it. Tap Detailed report and the real information opens up. Let's go through it in order. The score at the top Out of a hundred. A weighted average of several separate measurements; which ones count depends on the technique . This number does not measure whether your breathing was "correct". The only thing it measures is how closely you followed the pace on screen . It is perfectly possible to get a low score and feel very good, and the other way round. If you did the session without the microphone, no score is worked out. The measurements Length. How long you did and how long you planned. If you stopped early, it shows here. Cycles. How many full cycles you completed. Exhales heard. Something like "3 (target 4, on time 3)". The first number is how many exhales were heard, the second how many were expected, the third how many of those came at the right time. If the exhales heard are fewer than the target there are two possible reasons: either you really did miss a cycle, or your exhale was too quiet to be heard. To tell them apart, look at the technical lines below. Inhales heard. The inhale is far quieter than the exhale, and not hearing it is normal. Its share of the score is small. Holds. In techniques with a hold phase, in how many cycles no air escaped. When there is a leak, the reason is usually trying to lock the hold shut. Cycle restarts. How many times you restarted the cycle during the session. The technical lines These appear in full on the Advanced interface. Inhale level. How many decibels your inhale rose above your own silence. Close to zero means the inhale wasn't heard at all. Exhale peak level. The highest point of your exhale and the room's noise floor . Something like "20 dB above the floor (floor -66 dBFS)". This is the most useful line. If the difference is under 10 dB , your exhale is staying too quiet to be heard: bring the device closer. If the difference is over 40 dB , you are forcing the breath: let it go, don't push. Variation within the exhale. How much the sound moved during the exhale. A small number means a steady exhale; a large one means a broken or rasping exhale. The components The measurements that make up the score, each out of a hundred. Looking at which one is low tells you what to work on. If rhythm match is low , your exhales start late or early against the circle. The fix: wait for the moment the circle begins to shrink, and don't try to count. If exhales heard is low , either you missed some cycles or your exhale isn't being heard . If exhale length is low , your exhale is shorter or longer than the target. The most common cause is emptying too fast at the start: give less in the first second and spread the rest to the end. If exhale smoothness is low , the sound is coming out in bursts. Let the breath go in one piece. If breath volume is low , you are breathing out either too quietly or too loudly. The peak level line above tells you which. If completion is low , you didn't finish the session. Pick a shorter length next time. The buttons on the report screen Finish takes you back to the home screen and saves the session. Again starts the same technique for the same length straight away, with no trip through the technique picker. Every now and then a short feedback card follows the report: you rate the session out of ten and write a line or two if you feel like it. It can be skipped, and what gets sent is spelled out in the sharing article . The suggestions The sentences at the bottom of the report come from the measurements; they aren't random. If the same problem appears in several sessions in a row, it is worth working on. If you paused the session several times, a separate note about that appears too. What you see on the Simple interface If your interface level is Simple, the report shrinks to a single sentence. To see every measurement, set Interface to Standard or Advanced in Settings.

b: Reminders and notifications
o: The daily reminder, the streak alert, technique-specific notifications, the tone of the texts, quiet hours, holiday mode and the daily cap. What each one does and how to set it.
g: All the notifications live under Profile → Settings → Notification options . They are all scheduled on your device: nothing is pushed from a server. The daily reminder The most basic one. You can pick which day of the week and at what time, one by one — every day can have its own time. A day can hold more than one time, and a day left empty gets no reminder. If you'd rather not set them one by one, Make every day the same as Monday does it in a tap. A time is suggested from your answer to "when do you usually practise" in the intake , and you can change it afterwards. With Don't send if I've practised that day on, the evening reminder is dropped once you've done your morning session. It's on by default. If you have a program running, the daily reminder tells you the program's day as well. The streak alert The alert that comes when your streak is at risk — that is, when you haven't done a session that day and the day is nearly over. You choose the first alert time yourself. Whether it repeats is a separate setting: one alert, hourly, or down to every five minutes. The repeats stop as soon as you do the session. By default this alert sits outside your daily cap , so a full cap can't cost you your streak. You can count it towards the cap if you prefer. It doesn't land right after the daily reminder either: if the two are too close together, the app postpones the streak alert. Technique-specific notifications Separate reminders for particular moments: The Energizing Breath when you wake up 4-7-8 in the evening before bed The week's summary on Sunday evening On top of these there is a focus reminder during the day : it suggests an unlocked technique that suits the time of day. For the sleep and wake reminders you give a window — "earliest" and "latest". The notification lands somewhere inside it. These are turned on and off individually. If your health notes steer you away from a technique, that technique's notification can't be turned on at all , and the reason is written next to it. Lock and badge nudges Notifications that let you know when a new technique is close to unlocking, when an achievement is nearly in reach, or when a milestone is a day or two away. All three can be turned off separately. The unlock nudge also tells you which session to do: "one more Box Breathing session for Alternate Nostril", for instance. No nudge comes for techniques your health notes steer you away from. The tone and the sound Tone sets how the sentences read: Short , Motivating or Calm . The same notification arrives with a different sentence in each. Notification sound can be turned off; the notification still comes, quietly. Quiet hours The window when you don't want to be disturbed. No notification arrives during these hours. If a reminder you set yourself falls inside quiet hours, the app tells you and asks what you want to do. Holiday mode Silences every notification until a date you set. Your streak is frozen for that time: it neither breaks nor grows, and the counter stays where it is even if you do a session. You give the length by picking a date or with the ready-made buttons: three days, one week, two weeks. One warning: holiday mode ends an active program. Because a program keeps counting days. The app asks you about this before switching to holiday mode. To come out of holiday mode early, tap Cancel . If you cancel on the same day, the holiday counts as never used. If you take a long break There is a separate notification that nudges you back when you haven't practised for a while. You pick how often it comes: from once a day to once a week. It can be turned off. The daily cap You decide how many notifications can arrive in a day at most. If the cap is full when you try to turn on a new kind, the app warns you and offers a one-tap fix like "Raise the cap to 2 and turn it on" . Notification texts You can change the sentences used in notifications. There are sample texts, and you can write your own. If you want only your own text used, there is an option for that too. Recently sent notifications At the bottom of the settings there is a section showing the notifications sent recently. If you wonder why a notification arrived, you can look here. Resetting the settings If you've fiddled with everything and lost track, Reset notification settings puts it all back to the starting state: times, cap, quiet hours and the texts you wrote yourself. If you don't want notifications at all You can turn them all off. The app works completely without them; your streak, programs and milestones all carry on the same.

b: Setting up a program and keeping it
o: How to set up a twenty-eight day program, what happens when you miss a day, what an ended program means, and what you see when it finishes.
g: One session is one thing; keeping it up for weeks is another. A program is a structure that tracks doing the same technique for the same length every day. Where the programs are Profile → Programs. If the program's technique isn't unlocked, the menu shows as locked and tells you what is needed. Inside are cards you move through sideways. For now one program is published: 28-Day Physiological Sigh , five minutes a day. Setting one up Tap the card, tap Start program , and a setup screen opens: Daily length. The suggested value is five minutes. This isn't an arbitrary number — it is the length used in the study the program is based on. You can change it, but going below the suggested value means not doing the thing that was measured. Sessions per day. One or two. If you choose two, both have to be done for the day to count as complete. Start day. Today or a later date. If you pick a later date, the counter starts running on that day. Missed-day allowance. How many days in a row you can miss before the program ends. Set it tight and the program is strict, set it wide and it is forgiving; both are fair choices. Reminder time. If you have a daily reminder , it comes from there, and you can change it. While a program runs, your daily reminder also tells you the day: "Day 12 of your program". The daily flow The program's technique moves to the top of the technique list with "Program" written on it. You can start from there if you like. The shorter way: Do today's session on the Programs screen. Starting from here, the length picker doesn't appear at all — the session begins straight away at the program's length. When that day's session is complete, the card shows your progress: "12/28". If you miss a day Missing one day doesn't break the program. If you start missing days in a row, the app warns you: "Your program is about to end". Once you go past the missed-day allowance you set at the start, the program ends . An ended program isn't deleted; it goes to your history, and how far you got stays there. Turning on holiday mode ends the program — holiday mode silences notifications but doesn't stop the days from counting. You are asked about this plainly during setup. Leaving a program You can leave a program whenever you like: Leave program on the Programs screen. A program you leave is saved to your history. Programs that lasted at least three days appear in the history; shorter ones aren't saved. After leaving, a short question may come up: why you left. No score is asked for, only the reason — and it can be skipped. When it finishes When you complete the twenty-eighth day, a finishing screen appears: how many days, how many sessions and how many minutes you did, along with the All the Way achievement. On the way out of it, a feedback question may come up once. Looking at the history The history button on the Programs screen lists finished, ended and abandoned programs. Tap one and a detailed breakdown opens: A day-by-day calendar: which days were done, which slipped The numbers: days completed, days slipped, total sessions and minutes, longest unbroken run A breakdown by day of the week: "Tuesdays slipped most often" Scores: average, best, and the first half compared with the second The suggestions that came up most often over the program This breakdown gets simpler or fuller depending on your interface level .

b: Left Nostril and Right Nostril Breathing
o: In and out through one nostril. The two quietest techniques in the app, the difference between them, and where the evidence is weak.
g: Close one nostril lightly with a finger and breathe in and out through the other only. You don't switch sides — the same nostril stays open throughout. There are two separate techniques, and the difference between them is in the rhythm. Left Nostril: four in, six out The exhale is longer than the inhale. A long exhale helps the heart slow, so this technique sits on the calming side. Suited to the evening and before sleep. Right Nostril: four in, four out The inhale and exhale are equal. The calming effect is deliberately left out : this technique is for keeping alertness up. For the morning, or the dullness of the early afternoon. Done late in the day it can make falling asleep harder — the app reminds you of this at night. Where the evidence stands The studies on these two techniques measured single-nostril practice and reported different effects for the right and the left. The evidence is weak. Participant numbers are small and the results are waiting to be repeated. "The right nostril wakes you up, the left calms you down" is the best estimate we have, not a settled finding. The second values — why four, why six — aren't in the studies either. They were chosen from the slow-breathing literature. The suggested length in the app does come from the studies: the practice that was measured is twenty-seven breath cycles, and the suggested length is built from that. Going shorter in these techniques isn't "doing a bit less", it is not doing the thing that was measured. How it differs from the classical form The traditional form alternates: in through one nostril, out through the other. That is in the app too, called Alternate Nostril . The single-nostril form here is simpler, and it is the form the source studies measured. In the app they unlock before Alternate Nostril — getting used to one nostril makes the four-step alternating form easier. How to do it Sit comfortably. Press lightly on the side of the nostril you are closing — no force is needed to block it. Breathe in slowly through the open nostril for four seconds. Breathe out through the same nostril: six seconds on the left side, four seconds on the right. Don't release your finger. Common mistakes Switching nostrils. The two nostrils don't alternate in this technique. The same one stays open. Pressing hard enough to block the nose. Touching the side lightly is enough. Drawing in fast by force. Air passes slowly through one nostril; don't rush. How the app measures it These are the quietest techniques in the app. Both the inhale and the exhale are very low. The app knows this and uses its most sensitive thresholds for these two. Even so, not being heard is normal — you need to bring the device a little closer. Don't force the breath to make it audible. A forced single-nostril breath both spoils the technique and lowers the measurement. Who should take care If your nose is blocked, don't force it — pick another technique. No other known risk. Sources Raghuraj & Telles (2008), Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback — a study comparing right, left and alternate nostril breathing; twenty-one participants. PubMed Telles et al. (1994), Indian Journal of Physiology and Pharmacology — one of the early studies of single-nostril practice. Search PubMed

b: Streak, milestones and the calendar
o: How the streak works, which sessions count, how to set milestones of your own, and how to read the calendar.
g: There is a flame icon on the home screen with a number next to it: your streak . It shows how many days in a row you have done a session. Which sessions count towards the streak For a session to complete a day it has to be long enough . Sessions cut off after a few seconds don't count. Sessions without the microphone do count. Not getting a score has no effect on the streak. Doing several sessions in one day doesn't speed the streak up — it counts days, not sessions. A session that runs past midnight is recorded on the day it started . A session that begins at 23:50 and ends at 00:05 counts as yesterday's. Milestones There are stops along the streak: a few days, a week, a month and so on. When you reach one, it is celebrated on the home screen and in the session report . Besides the ready-made stops, you can set your own . Add a new goal from the streak screen and write in whatever number of days you like. It gets marked on the calendar and celebrated when you reach it. Stops you set yourself can be deleted. The calendar Tap the streak card on the home screen, or the Streak row in Profile, and the calendar opens. Every day is a box: days you did a session are filled, days you didn't are empty. Milestones are marked separately. Scroll up for previous months, and on to the year view. The year view shows the whole year on one screen — the regular stretches and the breaks stand out there. When the streak breaks Missing a day resets the streak. The app doesn't present this as a failure: your longest streak stays on record and a new streak begins the very next day. When you are already on your longest streak, the app doesn't tell you "your longest streak was X" — that sentence only appears when you are behind your record. Holiday mode If you are taking a break, turn on holiday mode : Settings → Notification options → Holiday mode . Notifications go quiet until the date you set, and your streak is preserved. Note: holiday mode ends an active program . Because a program keeps counting days. The streak alert If you haven't done a session that day and the day is nearly over, an alert arrives. You can set how many hours before the end it comes, or turn it off entirely. Not getting hung up on the streak A streak is a tool, not a debt. Giving up the app because you missed one day costs more than the missed day did. A two-minute session completes the day — on hard days, that is enough.

b: Choosing a technique and a length
o: What the marks on the technique list mean, what the lit band on the length slider is for, and the round selector that replaces length in Kapalabhati.
g: The list that opens when you tap Start isn't in a random order. Every mark on it means something. The marks on the cards " Suggested for you " and a turning light. The card at the top of the list. It is chosen from your goal, the time of day, your recent sessions and what you have already done today. It doesn't have to be the same every time you open it. "Program" and an amber light. If you have a program running and haven't done that day's session, the program's technique moves to the top and is marked in a separate colour. A yellow or red tint. There is a warning on that technique. Yellow is usually about the time of day ("not suitable for the night"); red is about your health notes or your age. The technique isn't hidden, only marked. A padlock and a number like "0/4". The technique isn't open yet. Tap it and it shows what is needed and the shortest way there. Cards that look faded. You are on the Simple interface and that technique isn't being suggested to you. The length slider The lit band above the slider is the range suggested for you. It is built from your experience, the scores of your recent sessions, your completion rate for that technique, the time of day and your streak. You don't have to stay inside the band — it is a suggestion, not a rule. As you drag your finger, a separate, more pronounced haptic tap marks the middle of the band. Once you pass the band, its colour changes behind the handle so you can see where you are. Underneath are preset buttons. For techniques with a program you can go up to ten minutes; for the others, up to five. On the Advanced interface, a line under the slider also tells you why the range is where it is . When a program takes over the length If you pick the technique of a program you have running, the length is locked: the program's daily length applies, and a line under the slider says so. If you start from Do today's session on the Programs screen , the length picker doesn't appear at all — you go straight into the session. Rounds instead of length in Kapalabhati In this technique you choose rounds , not length. One round means twenty-five fast breaths followed by half a minute of normal breathing. The presets are 1, 2, 3 and 5 rounds. You can also pick 4 by dragging the bar. If you have a health note, or if you are over sixty-five or under thirteen, the upper limit drops to 3 rounds and the reason is written under the round selector. The first session of the technique is always a single round, twenty breaths, and slower. Your own pace When you pick Coherent Breathing a line appears underneath: you can measure your own resonance pace and have Coherent run at it. Once measured, the value you found is used instead of five and a half seconds. Ignoring the suggestion All of this is a suggestion. If you want a different technique, pick it; take the length outside the band; you can do any un locked technique at any time. The app notes your choice and tunes its next suggestions accordingly.

b: What's on the session screen
o: The circle, the phase label, the sound wave, the short notes during a session, the microphone card and the pause menu. What everything you see during a session is for.
g: The session screen looks plain, but every part of it has a job. The countdown and the room measurement Before the session starts there is a three-second countdown. Right after it, the screen says "Measuring the room…" . Those few seconds matter: the app is measuring how quiet the room is, and the threshold for the whole session is set from it. Don't talk, don't move and don't reposition the device while it happens. The circle The circle in the middle of the screen plays the technique's rhythm. Breathe in as it grows. Out as it shrinks. Hold while it stays still. What you should be doing is written inside the circle, along with the seconds left in that phase. In techniques that use a single nostril, which nostril to breathe through is written here too. You don't have to count the circle — it is already counting. Your job is only to follow. The sound wave Under the circle there is a live wave. It shows what the microphone is hearing right now. If it moves when you breathe out, you are being heard. If it doesn't move at all, bring the device closer. If it keeps moving when you aren't breathing out, the room is noisy. The label next to it tells you what was detected: "Exhale detected" , "Inhale detected" , "Listening…" . Short notes during a session Every now and then a sentence appears under the circle and fades a few seconds later. These are things you can still fix before the session ends: "A little late. Breathe out as the circle shrinks." — your exhale starts after the circle. Start too early and the opposite note comes. "The exhale was short. Keep breathing out until the circle finishes shrinking." "Your breath is hard to hear." or the opposite, "Your breath is coming through very strong." The first asks you to bring the device closer, the second to move it away. "No sound on that exhale." — the target window for that cycle went by in silence. "Air escaped during the hold." — only in techniques with a hold. In Humming Bee Breath a separate note appears if the hum isn't heard. Good cycles get praise too: "Right on time." , "Rhythm's right, keep going." Those come after a few well-timed exhales in a row. How often they appear The notes are on a tight leash so they don't break the session. They never come during the first cycle or in the last seconds, there are at least ten seconds between two of them, the same sentence appears at most twice, and the total is scaled to the length of the session. In a short session you see one or two, and that's all. Why they never contradict the report The notes use the same threshold as the measurement behind the report . If a note said your breath wasn't heard, that exhale counts as unheard in the report too. And if the same note came up several times, it turns up again in the suggestions at the bottom of the report. The microphone card Unlike the short notes, this one stays on screen until you dismiss it. It appears in three situations: Your breath isn't being heard. Several exhale windows in a row went by in silence. It's too noisy here. The noise floor is high enough to make measuring hard. Too close. The exhale comes through so strongly that either the device is right in front of your face or you are blowing instead of breathing out. The card appears at most twice in a session. After the second one, a Continue without the microphone option appears. Haptics and the sound cue A short tap comes when the phase changes: you can tell that the inhale has started, or that you have moved to the exhale, without looking at the screen. For anyone who wants to do a session with their eyes closed, this is the real guide. If you like, a short tone can play at each phase change as well. Both are turned off in Settings: Session rhythm haptics and Sound cue . The pause menu Tap the pause button on screen and the session stops, opening a menu: Continue — carry on where you left off. Restart the cycle — starts the current cycle again; elapsed time is kept. End the session — finishes the session and goes to the report. To the left of the menu is the amount of time you have done so far. Pausing isn't a mistake, but it breaks the flow. If you paused several times, a note about it appears in the report. The Lock Screen and the Dynamic Island If you leave the app during a session, the session continues on the Lock Screen: the time left and the cycle appear there. On devices with a Dynamic Island, a small indicator stays at the top. This is for anyone who wants to put the phone down and close their eyes during a session: you don't need to watch the screen. A session without the microphone If you tap Continue without the microphone at the start, or the microphone is off, the circle, the haptics and the counter all work the same. Only the sound wave and the score are missing. You can switch mid-session as well: when the microphone card appears for the second time, a Continue without the microphone button shows up. The session carries on from where it was. It isn't scored, but it still counts towards your streak . Stopping a session early The report still arrives when you finish, and says how much you did. Sessions cut very short (a few seconds) aren't saved and don't count towards your streak.

b: Triangle Breathing
o: Four seconds in, four held, four out. The simplest technique with a hold, and where you first meet holds in the app.
g: Four seconds in through the nose. Hold for four. Four seconds out through the nose. Start the next cycle without waiting. Three steps, all equal. That is where the name comes from. What it is good for The hold slows the breath down. Four-four-four comes to five breaths a minute — inside the range where the measured effects of slow breathing are seen. Its second job is about attention. A counted rhythm gives the mind something to hold on to. In free breathing attention drifts easily; in counted breathing drifting becomes harder. That is why it helps before work that needs focus. Why before Box Box Breathing has two holds: one with full lungs and one with empty lungs. The second — waiting with empty lungs — feels harder than the first to most people, and it breaks the rhythm. Triangle is the version without that second hold. It is the gentlest way to meet holds. Once it starts to feel comfortable, moving to Box becomes easy; that is why the unlock order in the app runs from Triangle to Box. How to do it Sit upright, shoulders loose. Breathe in through the nose for four seconds, letting the belly rise. Hold for four seconds. Holding is not locking : don't close your throat, just stop the breath. Keep your shoulders and jaw loose. Breathe out through the nose for four seconds. As the exhale ends, move straight into the next inhale — there is no empty hold in this technique. Common mistakes Squeezing the breath into the chest during the hold. Hold loosely. If you feel pressure in your chest, you took in too much. Waiting after the exhale. If you are coming from Box Breathing this can be a reflex. In Triangle the next cycle starts the moment the exhale ends. Taking in more than fits in four seconds. You don't have to fill your lungs. Take in as much as you comfortably can in four seconds. How the app measures it The inhale and exhale are through the nose, so the sound is low — the thresholds are set for that. The hold phase is measured separately: if a sound is heard in that window, air is counted as having escaped, and it appears as its own line in the report. A small leak during the hold is normal in early sessions, and holding loosely rather than trying to lock it shut is what fixes it. Who should take care If you feel dizzy during a hold, skip the hold and breathe normally. The app doesn't hide this technique from anyone who marks a tendency to dizziness in the intake , but it does remind you that the hold can be skipped.

b: Unlocking techniques
o: What opens the locks, what a locked card tells you, and how to see the shortest way there.
g: Some cards in the technique list have a padlock on them. They aren't closed off, only not open yet : the app follows a path from easy to hard. Tap a locked card Tapping it opens a page showing what is needed. The technique's name at the top, and under it the requirements one by one with progress bars: > 2 Triangle — 1/2 > 2 Extended Exhale — 0/2 Under that, why this order is written out. For 4-7-8 , for instance: without experience of holds and long exhales, a seven-second hold can make you dizzy. The page also shows the shortest way : which technique to do to open this lock fastest. What counts Only scored sessions count: sessions without the microphone don't add to lock progress. Sessions cut very short don't count either. One session can count towards several locks at once. A requirement like "2 Coherent / Deep and Slow / Triangle" is satisfied by any of them. What sets the number of sessions Your experience level. If you said "I know some techniques" in the intake , the basic techniques are open from the start and the advanced ones open with half as many sessions. If you said "I'm experienced", most of the locks aren't there at all. The score of your introductory exercise. If the short exercise you did on the first day went well, the requirements drop. Score above ninety-five and one technique opens straight away. Your goal. Whatever you came for, that goal's technique starts unlocked. Say sleep and 4-7-8 is open; say focus and it's Box; say energy and it's the Energizing Breath . If your health notes steer you away from that technique, a different one opens for the goal — the app won't both say "I opened this for you" and put a warning on it. When a lock opens When a new technique opens, a short notice slides across the top of the home screen. Tap it and you go straight to that technique. Some screens have locks too: the Programs menu, the personal summary and the weekly summaries open after a certain point. They announce themselves the same way. If you don't want locks at all The locks exist to order the learning, not to punish. But if you came in already knowing the practice, marking your experience level honestly in the intake is the practical answer: choose "I'm experienced" and almost everything starts open. You can change it later too: Profile → Settings → Experience .

b: What we do with the data you share
o: If you turned on the anonymous session summary and audio samples, what those records come to us for, what happens to each one, and what becomes of them in the end.
g: There are two separate switches under Settings → Privacy: the anonymous usage summary and the occasional audio sample . Both arrive off, both are asked about separately, and both can be turned off whenever you like. If you didn't turn them on, nothing in this article happens on your device. If you did, here is what becomes of a record, step by step. What arrives With the anonymous summary on, this is what comes when a session ends: the technique, the length, the score and the report's numerical values — exhales heard, average exhale length, rhythm match, peak sound level, noise floor and so on. Alongside them, the device type and the app version. What doesn't come: your name, your email address, your identity, your location, your health answers from the intake , and your age. These never leave your device. The audio sample is a separate permission. With it on, the audio of at most five sessions a day is sent in compressed form and deleted from the device the moment it is sent . With the permission off, no audio is written to disk in any session. The feedback question that comes up now and then With anonymous sharing on, a short question appears at the end of a session now and then: a score out of ten , followed by one more question — depending on your score, "what didn't you like", "what could we improve" or "what did you like most". The second question names the technique you did. You can close it without giving a score. You can also give the score and leave without writing anything: the button at the bottom then says Send the score only , so not writing doesn't throw the score away. What is sent: the score you gave, the text you wrote , the technique, the length, the session score, whether the session was completed, whether the microphone was used, the app version and the date. Alongside them, the anonymous identifier above. What isn't sent is the same here: name, email address, identity, location, health answers, age. We read what you write — it is the only place that says what the numbers can't. So don't put your name, your email address or anything identifying in the box; if you want a reply, the right address is the support page . If you skip it, the app doesn't ask again for a while, and that wait grows with each skip; after a few skips it stops asking altogether. You are also asked once when you finish or abandon a program — the abandon question asks for no score, only the reason. If you didn't turn anonymous sharing on, this question never appears. What we do As records build up we ask one question: is what the app says true? We look for contradictions. Numbers that don't agree within the same session are the quickest clue. A report saying "every exhale was heard" while the same session shows an average exhale length of zero means something is wrong somewhere. We scan for these inconsistencies between measurements. We look at the distribution. When a value clusters outside what we expect, that is usually a threshold error. A real example: exhale peak levels were coming out systematically low on one family of devices — it turned out that on tablets the microphone sits on the device's far edge. We compare against the audio sample. When we have both the sound itself and the numbers the app produced for it, we can measure whether the detection is genuinely right: is there really an exhale where the app said "exhale", and did it miss any breaths. That is the audio sample's only job. We read the feedback by hand. Scores on their own don't get past "good/bad"; what is useful is the sentence next to them. When the same complaint comes from several people, it goes on the list. This article came out of exactly that. We fix it and test again. For every error we find, a test is written first — one that reproduces the error, based on the real recording we have. Then the fix is made. If the test passes, the change goes into the next release; if it doesn't, the fix was wrong. What we don't do No ads, no tracking, no third-party analytics tools. The records aren't sold, aren't handed to an ad network, and aren't transferred to another company. They aren't matched to an identity: we hold no link showing who sent which record. The records don't sit in your iCloud but in the app's shared database, and they are used only for the work described above. Changing your mind Both switches are turned off under Settings → Privacy. From the moment you turn them off, nothing more is sent. If you want what you sent earlier deleted, write to info@soluklan.app . Because the records aren't tied to an identity, we may ask for the dates you sent them so we can find yours.

b: Which technique, and when
o: Before sleep, during a work break, in a moment of anger, before a presentation. Which technique to pick for the situation, and why.
g: The app already suggests a technique, but it helps to know what to choose when you want something particular. Let's go situation by situation. Before sleep 4-7-8 or Extended Exhale . In both, the exhale is clearly longer than the inhale, and the heart slows on the exhale. 4-7-8 is stronger, but a seven-second hold doesn't suit everyone. If the hold feels hard, Extended Exhale does the same job with a shorter one. Left Nostril Breathing is also for the evening: through the left nostril only, four in and six out. Do it before you get into bed, not in it — keeping a lit screen in front of you doesn't help sleep. During a work break, to gather your attention Box Breathing or Triangle Breathing . A counted rhythm ties your attention to a single task. Two or three minutes is enough. These are the most useful right before a meeting or a piece of work that needs focus. In a moment of anger or tension The Physiological Sigh . One to three repeats is usually enough — this technique isn't meant to be sustained for minutes, it is for sudden tension. The body already does this by itself. Doing it deliberately means bringing that reflex forward. When you feel sleepy or dull The Energizing Breath . It is capped at one minute, and that is deliberate: fast breathing for longer can make you dizzy. Right Nostril Breathing is a gentler option: no fast breathing, just an even rhythm through the right nostril. Don't do either late in the day; the app warns you anyway. When your breathing feels tight Pursed Lip Breathing . This is the technique taught in pulmonary rehabilitation, developed for the feeling of breathlessness. It can be done without a screen while climbing stairs or when your breath gets tight: three seconds in through the nose, six seconds out through pursed lips. On a hot day Cooling Breath . Air drawn between the teeth leaves a clear coolness in the mouth. The feeling is real, but it doesn't lower your body temperature — that was measured, and it didn't drop. The coolness is in the mouth and throat. When your mind is scattered Alternate Nostril . Following the finger, the nostril and the rhythm at once leaves the mind no room for anything else. It is the technique in the app that demands the most coordination, which is why it is one of the last to unlock. When you just want to calm down Coherent Breathing or Deep and Slow . Neither has a hold, there is nothing to count, only a slow wave. For anyone new to breathing exercises these are the best start. That is why they are open from the beginning. For morning energy without fast breathing Kapalabhati is a stimulating technique, but it is also the one to approach most carefully. If you have a health note, the app steers you away from it. If none of the warnings apply to you and you are curious, the first session comes slow and single-round anyway. If you can't decide Take the suggestion at the top of the list. It is chosen from your goal, the time of day, your recent sessions and what you have done today — most of the time it is a sensible pick.

b: Widgets and Live Activity
o: Adding Home Screen and Lock Screen widgets, what each size shows, and the counter that appears on the Lock Screen during a session.
g: There are widgets for checking your streak without opening the app, or starting a session with one tap. The Home Screen widget Touch and hold an empty spot on your phone's (or tablet's) Home Screen, tap the plus at the top left, find Soluklan in the list and pick a size. Small: your streak and a one-tap start. Medium: your streak, how many days you have completed this week, and your next milestone . Large: all of that plus the progress of your running program and how far it is to the next stop. Tapping the widget opens the app and takes you straight to choosing a technique. The Lock Screen widget On the Lock Screen, touch and hold the clock, tap Customize , choose the Lock Screen and add Soluklan to the area under the clock. Your streak shows here. Tapping it opens the app. Live Activity If you leave the app during a session, the session continues on the Lock Screen: the time left and which cycle you are on are written there. On devices with a Dynamic Island a small indicator sits in the island, and tapping it returns you to the session. Here is where this earns its keep: you don't need to look at your phone during a session. The haptics already tell you the phases, so you can close your eyes and return to your breath — and if you do wonder, a glance at the Lock Screen is enough. If you haven't added a widget A short tip appears in the app once: a line telling you the widget exists. After you add one it doesn't appear again. The Your widgets section in Settings shows which ones you have added. If a widget isn't updating Widgets refresh at intervals iOS decides on, not instantly. After a session it can take a little while for the number to change. Opening and closing the app usually speeds it up.

b: Your first session, start to finish
o: Every step from opening the app for the first time to reading your first report. What you are asked, why you are asked it, and what to do where.
g: The first time you open the app you get a short intake. It takes less than a minute but it shapes everything that follows, so let's start there. 1. The intake There are seven questions. Every one can be skipped, but if you answer them the app sets itself up for you. Why are you here? Calm, focus, sleep, energy or "just trying it". This answer sets the order of the techniques and unlocks one that suits your goal right away. How familiar are you with breathing exercises? Four options, from "not at all" to "experienced". It sets how long the tutorials are and how many sessions the locks will ask for. How much time will you give a session? This becomes your default length . You can change it in every session. When do you usually practise? Suggestions are tuned to the time of day as well. You can also turn on the daily reminder from this screen. What age range are you in? Optional. Some techniques involve long holds and fast breathing, and the warnings follow from this. How should the interface be? Simple, Standard or Advanced. It sets how much information you see, and you can change it later. Any health notes? Asthma, heart, a tendency to dizziness, pregnancy. If you mark any, some techniques drop to the bottom of the list and a warning appears. This answer never leaves your device . At the end a short introductory exercise is suggested. You don't have to do it, but if you do, its score makes the locks easier. 2. Choosing a technique Tapping Start on the home screen opens the list of techniques. The card at the top says "Suggested for you" and has a light turning around it. It is chosen from your goal, the time of day and your recent sessions. Pick a different technique from below if you like. Locked techniques have a padlock and a progress marker like "0/4". Tap one and it shows you what is needed. 3. Choosing a length The slider under the card has a lit band on it: that is the range suggested for you . You don't have to stay inside it — it is only a suggestion. As you drag your finger, a separate haptic tap marks the middle of the band. There are preset buttons too (1 minute, 2 minutes, 3-5 minutes). For a first session, two minutes is a good start. 4. The tutorial If it is your first time with a technique, the tutorial comes first: what it is good for, how it is done step by step, and the mistakes people make. At the end there is a hands-on round . You do one cycle together with the microphone on, and the app confirms it can hear your breath. If you get stuck here, the step passes by itself after a few tries — you don't get trapped. To skip the tutorial, tap Skip at the top right. At the bottom of the intro screen there is a Don't show again box: tick it and that technique stops showing its intro. If you change your mind, Settings → Show tutorials again brings them all back. 5. The session A three-second countdown, then the room is measured — stay quiet while this happens, the app is measuring the noise in the room. Then the circle starts. Breathe in as it grows, out as it shrinks. What you should be doing is written inside the circle, along with the seconds left. There is a live sound wave at the bottom: it moves when your breath is heard. If it doesn't move at all, bring the device a little closer. To pause, tap Pause on screen. From the menu you can carry on, restart the cycle, or end the session. 6. The report When the session ends your report arrives: a score out of a hundred , a short headline, what you did well and a few suggestions. Tap Detailed report and you see every measurement one by one. In a first session this can feel like a lot — don't rush it. Over time you'll come to know what each line means. Tap Finish and you're back on the home screen, with your streak started. Three suggestions for the first days Keep it short. A finished two-minute session beats a five-minute one you abandon. Don't fixate on the score. A low score is normal in early sessions. The score measures how closely you followed the pace on screen, not whether your breathing was correct. Pick a quiet place. It makes the microphone's job easier, and the session easier too.
